tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3
2	
3	Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.
4	
5	One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
6	one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
7	file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
8	`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.
9	
10	## Terminology
11	
12	Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
13	under it.
14	
15	- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
16	- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
17	  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
18	  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
19	  in any open thread.
20	- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
21	  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
22	  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
23	- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
24	- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
25	  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
26	  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
27	- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
28	  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
29	  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
30	  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
31	  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
32	  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
33	- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
34	  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
35	- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
36	  eye, since the position already says it.
37	- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
38	  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
39	    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
40	    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
41	    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
42	  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
43	    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
44	    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
45	- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
46	  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
47	  the close.
48	- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
49	  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
50	  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
51	  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
52	- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
53	  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
54	  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
55	- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
56	  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
57	  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
58	  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
59	  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
60	  court until the answer comes.
61	- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
62	  Computed from the file alone.
63	- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
64	  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
65	  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
66	  thread naming the old id.
67	- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
68	  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
69	- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
70	  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
71	- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
72	  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
73	  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
74	  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
75	- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
76	  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
77	  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
78	- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
79	  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.
80	
81	## Read Actions
82	
83	### Read messages
84	
85	This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.
86	
87	1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
88	   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
89	   thread is the context to read it in.
90	2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.
91	
92	A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.
93	
94	### Find a thread
95	
96	Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.
97	
98	- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
99	- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
100	  its bodies.
101	- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
102	  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.
103	
104	## Write Actions
105	
106	Every write runs inside these guards, in order:
107	
108	- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
109	- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
110	- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
111	- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
112	- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.
113	
114	Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
115	the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.
116	
117	1. Take ownership.
118	2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
119	   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
120	3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
121	   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
122	   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
123	   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
124	   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
125	   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
126	   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
127	   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).
128	
129	### Fetch
130	
131	1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
132	2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
133	   working copy, and that is a write.
134	
135	### Open a thread
136	
137	1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
138	2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
139	   file when it has one.
140	
141	### Write a line
142	
143	Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
144	author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
145	by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
146	again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
147	is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
148	the reply links the outcome by sha-link.
149	
150	1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
151	2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
152	   it has one.
153	
154	### Close a thread
155	
156	The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
157	is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
158	and the close sits in the same commit.
159	
160	1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.
161	
162	## What is not here
163	
164	- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
165	  cannot disagree with the threads.
166	- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
167	- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
168	  and a reader takes what is there.
169	- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
170	  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
171	  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
172	  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
173	  and that is the change it would take.
174	- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
175	  participants, and history is the only recourse.
176	- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
177	  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
178	  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
179	  commit the rules require.
180	- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
181	  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
182	  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.
183	
184	## Versions
185	
186	The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
187	bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
188	under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
189	rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
190	the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.
191	
192	- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
193	  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
194	  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
195	  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
196	  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
197	- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
198	  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
199	  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
200	- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
201	  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
202	  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
203	  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
204	  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
205	  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
206	  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
207	  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
208	  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
209	  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
210	- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
211	  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
212	  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
213	  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.
214	
215	## Specimen

217	`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
218	and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the

1	# vc-x1 config file
2	
3	Configure the work-repo of a dual repo system. The other repo, we call the agent-repo, is
4	also a markdown configuration file typically named .vc-config.md.
5	
6	The code blocks in these config files are in toml format and these blocks are logically
7	concatenated in the order written here and those become the information used for configuring
8	the system. The [vc-config.md](vc-config.md) contains the documentation for the
9	various toml tables used for configuration and it is also used during compilation to define
10	the valid contents of this file.
11	
12	The file [vc-config-model.md](vc-config-model.md) is the model: every table and key a workspace
13	config may carry, each with its default or a typical value. It is generated from the schema, so it
14	cannot fall behind the keys the binary knows.
15	
16	The two repos
17	- work [[1]]
18	- agent [[2]]
19	```toml
20	[repos]
21	work = "."
22	agent = ".agent-session"
23	```
24	
25	The agent-repo's name on its remote, which clone and sync need when there is no agent-repo yet to
26	ask
27	- agent-repo [[9]]
28	```toml
29	[remote]
30	agent-repo = "vc-x1.agent-session"
31	```
32	
33	The agent-file family this repo belongs to: its member name and the sibling repos it answers to
34	- member [[3]]
35	- template [[4]]
36	- messages [[5]]
37	```toml
38	[family]
39	member = "vc-x1"
40	template = "../vc-x1-template/work"
41	messages = "../vc-x1-messages"
42	```
43	
44	The validation commands, each element one invocation, run in order by `vc-x1 validate`
45	- full [[6]]
46	- fast [[7]], `cargo test --bins` alone, the schema's example, wink's call 2026-10-20: the full
47	  list with plain `cargo test` measured the same 8 s as full, since the fourteen `dr1_*` fixture
48	  tests cost nothing once the fixture is built, so the only fast worth having skips fmt, clippy,
49	  the integration tests, and the install. Its trial of 2026-09-21 found a rung's failures in what
50	  it skips, so a rung's review still runs full

53	  and the test build full leaves is what the dev build then reuses

60	]
61	fast = ["cargo test --bins"]
62	```
63	
64	The build, one list for every profile, run in order with each element one invocation, a plain
65	`cargo build` naming the chosen profile's `Cargo.toml` profile, so its binary stays in `target/`
66	and nothing on the PATH is replaced until `vc-x1 install` copies it there, and `--locked` so every
67	profile's build compiles the same dependencies

69	  `{profile.cargo}` filled from the profile `--profile` names, else the default [[19]], release
70	```toml

73	```
74	
75	The install, one list for every profile, written out so the config says what `vc-x1 install` does.
76	It copies the binary to a `.new` file and then moves it into place, since a copy onto a running
77	binary fails and a move swaps it in whole, so a copy already running keeps the old code and the
78	next run gets the new. The list uses `{table.key}` placeholders, filled for the run, so each path
79	is written once, and `~` is expanded to the home directory, so the value fits every machine.
80	- dir [[11]], where every profile's binary goes, `~/.cargo/bin`
81	- commands [[12]], the install, the binary `{profile.bin}` under its file name with the profile's
82	  `{profile.suffix}` appended, so the dev build sits beside the release and never replaces it

85	dir = "~/.cargo/bin"

88	  "mv {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}.new {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}",

90	```
91	
92	The profiles `--profile` chooses among, each a `Cargo.toml` profile by its cargo [[13]] property,
93	its bin [[14]] the binary cargo leaves for it, and its suffix [[15]] what the installed name gets
94	- release, the default, installed as `vc-x1` at a cycle's Land
95	- dev, the debug build a rung tries, installed as `vc-x1-dev` beside it, wink's call 2026-10-21:
96	  after full's `cargo test` it reuses the test build and takes under a second against a release
97	  build's ten, forty against ten when cold, and its overflow checks and `debug_assert!` suit a
98	  build that exists to be tested

102	bin = "target/release/vc-x1"
103	
104	[profile.dev]
105	cargo = "dev"
106	bin = "target/debug/vc-x1"

111	commit --closing` needs no `--body` for a closing that says only where its record is
112	- body [[16]]

116	```

3	Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.
4	
5	One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
6	one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
7	file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
8	`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.
9	
10	## Terminology
11	
12	Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
13	under it.
14	
15	- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
16	- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
17	  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
18	  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
19	  in any open thread.
20	- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
21	  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
22	  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
23	- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
24	- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
25	  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
26	  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
27	- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
28	  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
29	  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
30	  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
31	  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
32	  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
33	- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
34	  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
35	- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
36	  eye, since the position already says it.
37	- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
38	  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
39	    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
40	    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
41	    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
42	  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
43	    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
44	    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
45	- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
46	  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
47	  the close.
48	- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
49	  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
50	  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
51	  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
52	- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
53	  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
54	  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
55	- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
56	  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
57	  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
58	  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
59	  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
60	  court until the answer comes.
61	- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
62	  Computed from the file alone.
63	- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
64	  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
65	  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
66	  thread naming the old id.
67	- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
68	  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
69	- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
70	  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
71	- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
72	  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
73	  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
74	  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
75	- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
76	  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
77	  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
78	- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
79	  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.
80	
81	## Read Actions
82	
83	### Read messages
84	
85	This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.
86	
87	1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
88	   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
89	   thread is the context to read it in.
90	2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.
91	
92	A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.
93	
94	### Find a thread
95	
96	Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.
97	
98	- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
99	- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
100	  its bodies.
101	- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
102	  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.
103	
104	## Write Actions
105	
106	Every write runs inside these guards, in order:
107	
108	- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
109	- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
110	- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
111	- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
112	- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.
113	
114	Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
115	the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.
116	
117	1. Take ownership.
118	2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
119	   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
120	3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
121	   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
122	   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
123	   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
124	   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
125	   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
126	   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
127	   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).
128	
129	### Fetch
130	
131	1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
132	2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
133	   working copy, and that is a write.
134	
135	### Open a thread
136	
137	1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
138	2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
139	   file when it has one.
140	
141	### Write a line
142	
143	Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
144	author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
145	by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
146	again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
147	is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
148	the reply links the outcome by sha-link.
149	
150	1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
151	2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
152	   it has one.
153	
154	### Close a thread
155	
156	The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
157	is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
158	and the close sits in the same commit.
159	
160	1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.
161	
162	## What is not here
163	
164	- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
165	  cannot disagree with the threads.
166	- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
167	- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
168	  and a reader takes what is there.
169	- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
170	  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
171	  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
172	  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
173	  and that is the change it would take.
174	- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
175	  participants, and history is the only recourse.
176	- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
177	  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
178	  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
179	  commit the rules require.
180	- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
181	  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
182	  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.
183	
184	## Versions
185	
186	The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
187	bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
188	under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
189	rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
190	the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.
191	
192	- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
193	  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
194	  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
195	  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
196	  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
197	- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
198	  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
199	  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
200	- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
201	  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
202	  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
203	  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
204	  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
205	  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
206	  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
207	  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
208	  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
209	  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
210	- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
211	  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
212	  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
213	  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.
214	
215	## Specimen
216	
217	`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
218	and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
219	lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
220	shown after it.
221	
222	```
223	# m-41 hello
224	- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
225	- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
226	- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
227	- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done
228	```
229	
230	````
231	# m-41-2 hey, and the cycle that answers it
232	
233	The cycle landed at
234	https://github.com/winksaville/def/blob/0123456789ab/TODO.md#feat-the-cycle.
235	
236	## What changed
237	
238	- one thing
239	- another, with the command that shows it:
240	
241	  ```
242	  vc-x1 validate --fast
243	  ```

  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

## Specimen

`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
shown after it.

```
# m-41 hello
- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done
```

````

  ```
  vc-x1 validate --fast
  ```

# vc-x1 config file

Configure the work-repo of a dual repo system. The other repo, we call the agent-repo, is
also a markdown configuration file typically named .vc-config.md.

The code blocks in these config files are in toml format and these blocks are logically
concatenated in the order written here and those become the information used for configuring
the system. The [vc-config.md](vc-config.md) contains the documentation for the
various toml tables used for configuration and it is also used during compilation to define
the valid contents of this file.

The file [vc-config-model.md](vc-config-model.md) is the model: every table and key a workspace
config may carry, each with its default or a typical value. It is generated from the schema, so it
cannot fall behind the keys the binary knows.

The two repos
- work [[1]]
- agent [[2]]
```toml
[repos]
work = "."
agent = ".agent-session"
```

The agent-repo's name on its remote, which clone and sync need when there is no agent-repo yet to
ask
- agent-repo [[9]]
```toml
[remote]
agent-repo = "vc-x1.agent-session"
```

The agent-file family this repo belongs to: its member name and the sibling repos it answers to
- member [[3]]
- template [[4]]
- messages [[5]]
```toml
[family]
member = "vc-x1"
template = "../vc-x1-template/work"
messages = "../vc-x1-messages"
```

The validation commands, each element one invocation, run in order by `vc-x1 validate`
- full [[6]]
- fast [[7]], `cargo test --bins` alone, the schema's example, wink's call 2026-10-20: the full
  list with plain `cargo test` measured the same 8 s as full, since the fourteen `dr1_*` fixture
  tests cost nothing once the fixture is built, so the only fast worth having skips fmt, clippy,
  the integration tests, and the install. Its trial of 2026-09-21 found a rung's failures in what
  it skips, so a rung's review still runs full
- full checks the source and makes no build to run, wink's call 2026-10-21: the dev build is
  `[build] dev` below, which `vc-x1 run --dev` runs first, so what runs is always the current code,
  and the test build full leaves is what the dev build then reuses
```toml
[validate]
full = [
  "cargo fmt",
  "cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings",
  "cargo test -- --include-ignored",
]
fast = ["cargo test --bins"]
```

The build, one list for every profile, run in order with each element one invocation, a plain
`cargo build` naming the chosen profile's `Cargo.toml` profile, so its binary stays in `target/`
and nothing on the PATH is replaced until `vc-x1 install` copies it there, and `--locked` so every
profile's build compiles the same dependencies
- commands [[10]], the build, run by `vc-x1 build` and first by `vc-x1 run` and `vc-x1 install`,
  `{profile.cargo}` filled from the profile `--profile` names, else the default [[19]], release
```toml
[build]
commands = ["cargo build --profile {profile.cargo} --locked"]
```

The install, one list for every profile, written out so the config says what `vc-x1 install` does.
It copies the binary to a `.new` file and then moves it into place, since a copy onto a running
binary fails and a move swaps it in whole, so a copy already running keeps the old code and the
next run gets the new. The list uses `{table.key}` placeholders, filled for the run, so each path
is written once, and `~` is expanded to the home directory, so the value fits every machine.
- dir [[11]], where every profile's binary goes, `~/.cargo/bin`
- commands [[12]], the install, the binary `{profile.bin}` under its file name with the profile's
  `{profile.suffix}` appended, so the dev build sits beside the release and never replaces it
```toml
[install]
dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
commands = [
  "cp {profile.bin} {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}.new",
  "mv {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}.new {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}",
]
```

The profiles `--profile` chooses among, each a `Cargo.toml` profile by its cargo [[13]] property,
its bin [[14]] the binary cargo leaves for it, and its suffix [[15]] what the installed name gets
- release, the default, installed as `vc-x1` at a cycle's Land
- dev, the debug build a rung tries, installed as `vc-x1-dev` beside it, wink's call 2026-10-21:
  after full's `cargo test` it reuses the test build and takes under a second against a release
  build's ten, forty against ten when cold, and its overflow checks and `debug_assert!` suit a
  build that exists to be tested
```toml
[profile.release]
cargo = "release"
bin = "target/release/vc-x1"

[profile.dev]
cargo = "dev"
bin = "target/debug/vc-x1"
suffix = "-dev"
```

The closing commit's default body, `{title}` the cycle title read from the opening, so `vc-x1
commit --closing` needs no `--body` for a closing that says only where its record is
- body [[16]]
```toml
[closing]
body = 'Closes the cycle "{title}". See details in TODO.md.'
```

The acceptance-test fixtures, one dual workspace per name under the directory, inside the
workspace and gitignored, so a fresh clone builds or fetches its own there and the committed config
names no path on one machine
- fixtures [[8]]
```toml
[test]
fixtures = ".fixtures"
```

# References

[2]: vc-config.md#reposagent
[3]: vc-config.md#familymember
[4]: vc-config.md#familytemplate
[5]: vc-config.md#familymessages
[6]: vc-config.md#validatefull

[8]: vc-config.md#testfixtures

[11]: vc-config.md#installdir
[12]: vc-config.md#installcommands
[13]: vc-config.md#profilenamecargo
[14]: vc-config.md#profilenamebin
[15]: vc-config.md#profilenamesuffix
[16]: vc-config.md#closingbody
[19]: vc-config.md#builddefault-profile

content.content:
60	## Todo format
61	
62	`TODO.md` has these sections, in this order. Each item in them is a short description with
63	reference links to more detail.
64	
65	- `## Continuation notes`: where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a
66	  record, `_None._` by default, written before a restart or a loss of context, and reset by the
67	  agent that reads it, after filing each fact into its home or keeping the bullet whose fact has
68	  none, so a reset never destroys the only copy of anything.
69	- `## In Progress`: the running cycle's record ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
70	- `## Waiting`: important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on and its
71	  rank once unblocked, and every opening checks the conditions.
72	- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in
73	  [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md).
74	- `## Ideas`: unranked.
75	- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).
76	- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
77	- `# References`: the file-local reference definitions, the file's last section ([Reference
78	  numbering](#reference-numbering)).
79	
80	Every adopter has one `TODO.md` of this shape. It is not an agent-file, since its content is the
81	project's record, and `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh` ships it as a skeleton: `## In Progress` reading
82	`_No cycle currently in progress._`, the other sections empty.
83	
84	An entry is a `###` heading, its title, followed by its text. Priority is file order, the first
85	entry the highest, and reprioritizing is moving the entry. The title is unique within its file and
86	is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
87	verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
88	renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
89	form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
90	bold title, cited by the bold text.
91	
92	Example shape:
93	
94	```
95	## Todo
96	
97	### Add new feature X
98	
99	The feature, in a sentence or two ([details](features.md#feature-x)).
100	
101	### Fix bug Y
102	
103	What is wrong and where [[1]].
104	
105	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
106	```
107	
108	## The In Progress block
109	
110	A cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
111	([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), finalized and moved to `## Closed` by the closing commit, and
112	deleted by the next opening ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). The picked-up `## Todo`
113	item is moved here (never copied) and becomes the cycle-record's **provisional items**, all
114	required, all revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the
115	other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
116	under a program heading, each one deeper):
117	
118	- **title**, the cycle's name, what `git log --grep` finds it by
119	- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
120	- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's commit
121	  body carries the final one
122	- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can run
123	  it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed check is
124	  one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
125	- **deliberation**: how the other five were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
126	  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
127	  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
128	  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
129	  answer
130	- **rungs**: a `#### Rungs` heading over the rung subsections, the ladder itself being `zTOC.md`'s
131	  ([zTOC format](#ztoc-format)): one rung per step, `- 2 (done) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)`: the
132	  rung's version suffix, which `-V` and the installed dev build print, then the marker, `(done)` or
133	  `(current)`, both first so they read down their columns, and a rung not yet started has neither,
134	  its suffix being set when its commit bumps the version, and an inline link so the ladder is one
135	  list with nothing beside it to keep in step, its line as long as the title makes it. `<title>` is
136	  the rung's commit title, `<type>: <desc>` per [Conventional-commit
137	  shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit), so a moved `## Todo` entry is retitled.
138	  The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`, is linked like the rest
139	
140	`#### Rungs` holds the **rung subsections**, one per rung in the ladder's order, the closing
141	included, headed by the rung's exact title, so the ladder is their index. Each opens at laddering
142	with an abstract-sized intent statement (the rung's problem and solution in a sentence or two) and
143	completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual delta: design points, consequences, deferrals,
144	never a restatement of the landed commit body. The closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out
145	the cycle." and completes at close-out with what closing taught, in problem/solution form, or
146	`_None._`.
147	
148	A rung is `- N (marker) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title
149	links to the rung's subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
150	numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
151	SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
152	that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.
153	
154	A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- N (marker) <cycle title>`, with no subsection
155	under it: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's anchor ([Cycle
156	shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
157	
158	The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
159	`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
160	
161	## zTOC format
162	
163	`zTOC.md`, beside `TODO.md` at the work-repo root, is the workspace's index, so the running ladder
164	and the files worth knowing are found without reading `TODO.md`'s length, and the `z` sorts it last
165	in a listing. Its sections, in this order:
166	
167	- `# TOC`, the title.
168	- `## Ladder`: the cycle's ladder, its one copy, each rung with its marker as [The In Progress
169	  block](#the-in-progress-block) shapes it, linking across to its subsection in `TODO.md`, since a
170	  same-file link does not work in every markdown preview, zed's among them. Written at the opening,
171	  replacing the last cycle's, its markers set by the per-rung flow, and kept by the closing commit,
172	  so the landmark's tree holds the finished ladder beside its `## Closed`.
173	- `## The TOC`: one link per file worth knowing, with what it holds, `TODO.md` first.
174	
175	Its links are inline, so it has no `# References`.
176	
177	Like `TODO.md` it is not an agent-file, and `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh` ships it as a skeleton, `##
178	Ladder` reading `_None._` until the first opening.
179	
180	## Frozen history: chores and done
181

- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in

- `## Ideas`: unranked.
- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).
- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
- `# References`: the file-local reference definitions, the file's last section ([Reference

Example shape:

```
## Todo

### Add new feature X

### Fix bug Y

What is wrong and where [[1]].

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
```

## The In Progress block

A cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), finalized and moved to `## Closed` by the closing commit, and
deleted by the next opening ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). The picked-up `## Todo`

other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
under a program heading, each one deeper):

- **title**, the cycle's name, what `git log --grep` finds it by
- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's commit
  body carries the final one
- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can run
  it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed check is
  one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
- **deliberation**: how the other five were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
  answer
- **rungs**: a `#### Rungs` heading over the rung subsections, the ladder itself being `zTOC.md`'s
  ([zTOC format](#ztoc-format)): one rung per step, `- 2 (done) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)`: the
  rung's version suffix, which `-V` and the installed dev build print, then the marker, `(done)` or
  `(current)`, both first so they read down their columns, and a rung not yet started has neither,
  its suffix being set when its commit bumps the version, and an inline link so the ladder is one
  list with nothing beside it to keep in step, its line as long as the title makes it. `<title>` is
  the rung's commit title, `<type>: <desc>` per [Conventional-commit
  shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit), so a moved `## Todo` entry is retitled.
  The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`, is linked like the rest

`#### Rungs` holds the **rung subsections**, one per rung in the ladder's order, the closing
included, headed by the rung's exact title, so the ladder is their index. Each opens at laddering
with an abstract-sized intent statement (the rung's problem and solution in a sentence or two) and
completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual delta: design points, consequences, deferrals,
never a restatement of the landed commit body. The closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out
the cycle." and completes at close-out with what closing taught, in problem/solution form, or
`_None._`.

A rung is `- N (marker) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title
links to the rung's subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.

A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- N (marker) <cycle title>`, with no subsection
under it: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's anchor ([Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).

## zTOC format

`zTOC.md`, beside `TODO.md` at the work-repo root, is the workspace's index, so the running ladder
and the files worth knowing are found without reading `TODO.md`'s length, and the `z` sorts it last
in a listing. Its sections, in this order:

- `# TOC`, the title.
- `## Ladder`: the cycle's ladder, its one copy, each rung with its marker as [The In Progress
  block](#the-in-progress-block) shapes it, linking across to its subsection in `TODO.md`, since a
  same-file link does not work in every markdown preview, zed's among them. Written at the opening,
  replacing the last cycle's, its markers set by the per-rung flow, and kept by the closing commit,
  so the landmark's tree holds the finished ladder beside its `## Closed`.
- `## The TOC`: one link per file worth knowing, with what it holds, `TODO.md` first.

Its links are inline, so it has no `# References`.

Like `TODO.md` it is not an agent-file, and `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh` ships it as a skeleton, `##
Ladder` reading `_None._` until the first opening.

## Frozen history: chores and done

# Cycle model

A cycle's `## In Progress` block, shown as a specimen rather than a skeleton: the `config loader`
cycle, mid-run, with its opening landed and its first work rung current. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [The In Progress block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).

One thing the specimen cannot show:

- a single-step cycle drops both bookends and all the steps are in the one commit: the ladder is one
  unlinked rung with the bare title, and there are no rung subsections under it ([Cycle
  shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

## In Progress

### refactor: extract config loader

#### Problem

Config parsing lives inside the CLI entry point, so every subcommand that wants a setting reaches
through `main` for it, and a test cannot load a config without building the CLI.

#### Solution

Move config loading into its own module with a single `load` entry point that the CLI and the tests
call alike.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with a new test that loads a config from a fixture file without touching `main`,
and `vc-x1 config --validate` reports the same findings as before the move.

#### Deliberation

- one work rung, not two: the parser and the loader were going to be split first and moved second,
  but the move is what forces the split, so doing them together is fewer edits
- the acceptance check compares `config --validate` output rather than asserting on internals, so a
  later rename inside the module does not invalidate it

#### Rungs

The rung subsections, in the ladder's order. The ladder itself is in `zTOC.md > ## Ladder`.

##### refactor: extract config loader opening

The cycle's setup commit: create the bookmark, delete `## Closed`'s contents, move the
Todo entry into this block, and bump the version-of-record.

##### refactor: split loader from parser

Loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load without parsing and a test cannot parse
without a file on disk.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config/loader.rs` finds and reads the file, returning the text and its path, so a caller that
    only wants to know which file was read stops here.
  - `config/parser.rs` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands it a string and never
    touches the filesystem.
    - the error type stays shared for now, since splitting it would change the messages
      `config --validate` prints and the acceptance check compares them
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field access moves behind the module
    boundary and the CLI no longer knows the file's shape.

##### refactor: extract config loader closing

Closing out the cycle.

The same cycle's ladder, `zTOC.md > ## Ladder`, its one copy, linking across to the subsections

- 1 (current) [refactor: split loader from parser](TODO.md#refactor-split-loader-from-parser)
