398:## Working practices
399-
400-**One command per shell invocation** because bundling hides which step produced which output.
401-
402-**Never mask a command's exit status**: a pipeline's status is the last command's, so a validating
403-command piped into `tail` / `grep` reports the filter's success, not its own. A trailing
404-`; echo "exit=$?"` prints the status while the invocation itself still exits 0, so the failure is
405-visible only to whoever reads the text. `failed=$rc` stays unquoted because it has no spaces to
406-protect, and the quotes can stop a harness permission rule from matching a command it would
407-otherwise allow (wink, 2026-08-05). One form, bare and last, since the Bash tool reports a nonzero
408-exit itself, so a printed status is never needed, and one form is easier to keep than three
409-(wink, 2026-10-27).
410-
411-**Hooks guard the exit-status rule** (wink, 2026-10-27): the rule held on paper and was broken
412-through a whole session by a trailing `; echo rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}`, because nothing failed when it
413-slipped and the user caught it by reading. `bash-guard.sh` makes the slip fail, with two text
414-matches, each a deny whose reason is the rule's form. Joins are left to the rule, since the
415-agent's commands carry heredocs and quoted programs whose `;` only a shell parser tells apart, and
416-a guard that stops legitimate scripts gets removed. Matching hooks run in parallel and `deny` wins
417-over `bash-allow.sh`'s `allow` (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, PreToolUse decision
418-control). The hooks are in the set so they travel with the rules they serve.
419-
420-**Use https remotes, not ssh.** Unconditional rather than "when the agent is sandboxed" because the
421-remote is chosen at clone time and whether a sandboxed agent will ever touch the repo is not
422-knowable then. A sandbox denies ssh twice over: reads of `~/.ssh` are blocked except the signing key
423-and `known_hosts`, so no auth key is available, and we think a host allowlist cannot admit port 22
424-at all, since ssh carries no SNI or Host header to match on. The network leg is a spawned `git`
425-child that inherits the sandbox, which is why the same config succeeds from a human's terminal and
426-fails from a session. Both wrong theories (size, timeouts) were held, and eliminated by test, before
427-the rule was written. Changing a remote's URL needs the user's go because it moves where the repo
428-publishes.
429-
430-**Delegate mechanical subtasks to lesser models** because top-model tokens are the scarce resource.
431-**Don't use the per-project memory directory** because easy for everyone to find beats convenient
432-for the agent alone. **Mark speculation** so a reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
433-
434-### A session's rules are its own agent-files

437-under that repo's own protocol alone (2026-08-30): it read the sibling's README as displacing

content.text:
The list is the right skeleton. Here is what I'd question or add, biggest first.

1. **There is no path back from "test cycle".** If the test finds a fault after the closing commit, the list has nowhere to go. I'd make the closing redoable while it is local: drop it, add a rung, close again, test again. Once the closing is pushed, a fault is a new rung plus a new closing, or a new cycle. This choice shapes the commands more than anything else on the list.

2. **"Test cycle" tests what lands only if the land is a fast-forward.**
   - A trapezoid closing already contains the merge with the target, so "merge/land" is only a bookmark move.
   - A linear closing whose target has moved needs a merge or rebase at land, which creates a commit nobody tested.
   - I'd make the land fast-forward only, always. If the target moved, close again and retest. The last step then reads "land", not "merge/land".

3. **The two closing decisions are one.** "Other commits to incorporate" and "list of parents" are both the parent list: each head joined is a parent, and the target as first parent is what makes it a trapezoid. That matches your `--closing [REV,...] --trapezoid <T>` design.

4. **The acceptance check has a chicken-and-egg problem.** The closing commit records the check's result, but "test cycle" runs after that commit. I'd split it:
   - The acceptance check runs on the last work rung and is recorded by the closing.
   - "Test cycle" is validation of the closed tree, which only matters when the merge brought in target changes.

5. **The open step, third bullet.** "Add In Progress to Closed" reads like the closing's job. I assume you mean "move the Todo entry into In Progress"; correct me if not. Since `vc-x1 open` does only the bookmark today, it could also do the other two bullets plus the ladder scaffold and the version bump. Those are mechanical and are where an agent drifts.

6. **Deliberating before the opening commit is good.** It is what we just did, and the opening then carries the plan instead of a stub. It should be written into the protocol, which today treats the opening as bookkeeping.

7. **Missing steps.** Some may be deliberately below this level:
   - Sync at open, before the closing, and before the land.
   - The per-rung bump and marker, and the dev install before review.
   - The agent-repo half of each commit and push.
   - Deleting the cycle's bookmark, locally and on `origin` if it was pushed.
   - Installing the release build after the land.
   - Continuation notes.
   - The dead-end exit.

8. **Single-step cycles.** The list implies every cycle has an opening commit and a closing commit. One shape is easiest to follow consistently, at the cost of two commits for a one-line fix. The alternative is to make the opening commit optional, with a closing that carries everything when there is none. That is a decision to make explicitly, since today's finalize-in-place is the special case that surprised you in `wt-21-6`.

9. **Three push points, two different pushes.** The rung and cycle pushes publish the cycle's bookmark as a draft. The last one publishes the target and removes the draft. Naming them differently in the protocol would stop one being mistaken for the other.

The plain version: the list works going forward, but it needs a way back when the final test fails, and the land should never create a commit that was not tested.

104	## vc-x1 commit and push: what they do and do not do
105	
106	`vc-x1 commit -s b --title "..." --body "..."` commits both repos with the title and body, the
107	pair, stamps their trailers ([above](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)), and stays on this
108	machine. `-s w` commits the work repo alone, its trailer naming the agent `@`. `--push` publishes
109	what was committed, as `vc-x1 push` does, and `vc-x1 show -s work -r @-` is the look at it before
110	then. `-r` names a commit below `@`, described in place with its trailer stamped, and `--bookmark`
111	the bookmark to advance. Every argument is a flag. What to keep in mind:
112	
113	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 runs no build or tests. Validation is the per-rung
114	  flow's job, run *before* the commit.
115	- **Rerunning a push is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume: every stage no-ops when its
116	  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed.
117	- **The trailers are stamped**, never hand-written into `--title` or `--body`.
118	- **The agent-repo is a linear journal.** Never create an agent-repo bookmark mirroring a work-repo
119	  one: it steers session pushes at the wrong remote ref.
120	
121	A late work-repo tweak after a push (a forgotten edit) is folded by `vc-x1 squash` and re-pushed,
122	which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push. Pushing is not what makes a commit
123	history: `squash` warns of a published commit jj counts mutable, a cycle's bookmark pushed for a
124	backup among them, and refuses one in jj's `immutable()`, `main@origin`, tags, and what the user's
125	`immutable_heads()` adds, without `--ignore-immutable`, as jj refuses it.
126	
127	## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
128	
129	**Never `jj describe` a commit that already carries trailers, and never re-describe a published one
130	without coordinating with everyone involved first**
131	([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
132	and by hand it silently drops the cross-repo link. `vc-x1 squash --title --body` is the sanctioned
133	re-describe of `@-`, keeping the trailers. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
134	described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not
135	covered. That is a [local ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe. `vc-x1 fix-desc`
136	repairs a dropped trailer by title match.
137	
138	## Cycle bookmarks: create and land
139	
140	The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
141	holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
142	([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
143	
144	**Create**, first at the cycle's opening: `vc-x1 open --title "<bare cycle title>"` makes the
145	bookmark on the work `@`, named by the title's slug (the anchor algorithm in [Markdown anchor
146	links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)), or `--bookmark <NAME>`, and kept local. It refuses a name
147	in use, locally or on `origin`, and nothing else, `@` holding edits or not. The bookmark follows the
148	change, so `vc-x1 commit -s b --opening --title "<bare cycle title>" --body "..."` commits the
149	opening on it, creating none, and refuses an `@` without it.
150	
151	**Close**: `vc-x1 commit -s b --closing <BM|REV> --onto <BOOKMARK>`, naming the cycle's tip and its
152	target, makes the closing: the merge of the target and the tip, the one commit finalized in place,
153	or, with nothing committed above the target, the one commit made from `@`, `--title` and `--body`
154	given. No target is assumed, and a closing without `--onto` is refused naming the bookmark below the
155	opening. Without a `[closing] body` in `.vc-config.md`, it needs `--body`.
156	
157	**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Its `vc-x1
158	push` is the push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push), with the closing words
159	before it and silence after ([At rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest)):
160	
161	1. Sync: `vc-x1 sync -s b`, and a `main` it moved stops the Land ([Sync](../AGENTS.md#sync)).
162	2. Integrate: `vc-x1 land -s b --onto <target>`, local: it commits the agent `@` as the partner of
163	   the work commits that name it, none when every rung is a pair, fast-forwards the target, and
164	   deletes the cycle's local bookmark, every check made first.
165	   `--dry-run` says each step. The user may test here, before anything is published.
166	3. Publish: `vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark <target>`, the work repo first, the journal folded into the
167	   last agent commit while that is unpublished. `land --push` does steps 2 and 3 as one.
168	   The agent publishes only with the user's permission, and otherwise the user does after the
169	   session, by `vc-x1 squash-push -s b` ([At rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest)).
170	4. Remote bookmark: `vc-x1 delete-bookmark -s w --bookmark <bookmark> --skip local`, when the topic
171	   was ever pushed.
172	5. Install: `vc-x1 build`, a `vc-x1 run -- -V` smoke check, and `vc-x1 install`, so the plain name
173	   is replaced only by what is on the target.
174	
175	- `vc-x1 land --onto` another cycle's bookmark, a stack of cycles landing together, is the command
176	  and not the sequence: nothing is installed, and the cycle is permanent only when the stack lands
177	  on its target.
178	- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
179	  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.
180	- `vc-x1 land` only fast-forwards. A target that moved means the closing is made again, as its merge
181	  has to join the target where it is.
182	
183	**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
184	bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):
185	
186	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
187	  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
188	  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
189	- **A topic that was pushed is force-pushed**, under the same approval as any other push.
190	
191	## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged
192	
193	A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
194	carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
195	holder.
196	
197	- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
198	- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
199	- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the known
200	  cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive a rebase
201	- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and is deleted,
202	  locally and remotely
203	
204	The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten
205	freely until it lands (see [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)), this
206	one is published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never
207	rebased" wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.
208	
209	## Close-out shapes
210	
211	The shape a ladder lands in is carried by its closing commit, so nothing is reshaped at
212	[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle is
213	one commit and lands as it is:
214	
215	- **trapezoid**: a merge commit whose first parent is the target and whose second is the ladder, so
216	  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung stays reachable. It joins a
217	  target that moved. With one rung the figure is a triangle.
218	- **linear**, one commit per rung on the target, is proposed as `--shape linear` and not built. We
219	  think it refuses a target that moved, since joining one would rewrite the reviewed ladder.
220	
221	Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
222	rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
223	shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
224	
225	**Preview before closing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
226	whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
227	described in
228	[Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context).

holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).

**Create**, first at the cycle's opening: `vc-x1 open --title "<bare cycle title>"` makes the
bookmark on the work `@`, named by the title's slug (the anchor algorithm in [Markdown anchor
links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)), or `--bookmark <NAME>`, and kept local. It refuses a name
in use, locally or on `origin`, and nothing else, `@` holding edits or not. The bookmark follows the
change, so `vc-x1 commit -s b --opening --title "<bare cycle title>" --body "..."` commits the
opening on it, creating none, and refuses an `@` without it.

**Close**: `vc-x1 commit -s b --closing <BM|REV> --onto <BOOKMARK>`, naming the cycle's tip and its
target, makes the closing: the merge of the target and the tip, the one commit finalized in place,
or, with nothing committed above the target, the one commit made from `@`, `--title` and `--body`
given. No target is assumed, and a closing without `--onto` is refused naming the bookmark below the
opening. Without a `[closing] body` in `.vc-config.md`, it needs `--body`.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Its `vc-x1
push` is the push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push), with the closing words
before it and silence after ([At rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest)):

1. Sync: `vc-x1 sync -s b`, and a `main` it moved stops the Land ([Sync](../AGENTS.md#sync)).
2. Integrate: `vc-x1 land -s b --onto <target>`, local: it commits the agent `@` as the partner of
   the work commits that name it, none when every rung is a pair, fast-forwards the target, and
   deletes the cycle's local bookmark, every check made first.
   `--dry-run` says each step. The user may test here, before anything is published.
3. Publish: `vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark <target>`, the work repo first, the journal folded into the
   last agent commit while that is unpublished. `land --push` does steps 2 and 3 as one.
   The agent publishes only with the user's permission, and otherwise the user does after the
   session, by `vc-x1 squash-push -s b` ([At rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest)).
4. Remote bookmark: `vc-x1 delete-bookmark -s w --bookmark <bookmark> --skip local`, when the topic
   was ever pushed.
5. Install: `vc-x1 build`, a `vc-x1 run -- -V` smoke check, and `vc-x1 install`, so the plain name
   is replaced only by what is on the target.

- `vc-x1 land --onto` another cycle's bookmark, a stack of cycles landing together, is the command
  and not the sequence: nothing is installed, and the cycle is permanent only when the stack lands
  on its target.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.
- `vc-x1 land` only fast-forwards. A target that moved means the closing is made again, as its merge
  has to join the target where it is.

**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
- **A topic that was pushed is force-pushed**, under the same approval as any other push.

## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged

A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
holder.

- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the known
  cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive a rebase
- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and is deleted,
  locally and remotely

The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten
freely until it lands (see [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)), this
one is published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never
rebased" wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.

## Close-out shapes

The shape a ladder lands in is carried by its closing commit, so nothing is reshaped at
[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle is
one commit and lands as it is:

- **trapezoid**: a merge commit whose first parent is the target and whose second is the ladder, so
  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung stays reachable. It joins a
  target that moved. With one rung the figure is a triangle.
- **linear**, one commit per rung on the target, is proposed as `--shape linear` and not built. We
  think it refuses a target that moved, since joining one would rewrite the reviewed ladder.

Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

**Preview before closing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
described in
[Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context).

#### Flow

(wink + agent, 2026-11-11) The cycle as a list of operations, wink's, with every sub-step we could
name, so each can be sorted into what `vc-x1` does and what is done by hand. The goal is simplicity
for users and agents, with the steps still separable, so we or others can change the flow. A draft
the deliberation revises, the questions it raises being in the list after it.

The mark on a sub-step says who does it:

- (tool): a `vc-x1` command does it today.
- (tool?): mechanical and done by hand today, a candidate for `vc-x1`.
- (hand): a judgment, the user's or the agent's, which stays by hand.

1. Open:
   - (tool) Sync both repos, `vc-x1 sync -s b`, and stop on a repo held back.
   - (hand) Fetch and read the messages repo, where a workspace has one.
   - (hand) Choose the `## Todo` entry and its cycle title, a Conventional Commit.
   - (tool) Create the bookmark on the work `@`, `vc-x1 open --title`.
   - (hand) Check each `## Waiting` condition and promote what is met.
   - (tool?) Delete what `## Closed` holds, and the reference definitions only it used.
   - (tool?) Move the `## Todo` entry into `## In Progress` as a scaffold: the title heading, the
     item headings, the entry's text under Problem, and the opening and closing rung subsections.
   - (tool?) Replace `zTOC.md`'s ladder with the opening, marked `(current)`, and the closing.
   - (tool?) Bump the version-of-record to the opening's suffix, and the lock file with it.
2. Deliberate and plan the cycle:
   - (hand) Write the problem, the solution, the acceptance check, and the deliberation.
   - (hand) Ladder the work rungs, each a title in `zTOC.md` and a subsection of intent.
3. Commit the cycle opening:
   - (tool) Validate, `vc-x1 validate`.
   - (tool) Install the dev build when the artifact changed, `vc-x1 install --profile dev`.
   - (hand) Review of the working-copy diff, "please review" and the user's go.
   - (tool?) Flip the opening's marker to `(done)`.
   - (tool?) Title and body: the cycle title plus " opening" and a pointer body, defaults the
     tool could supply as the closing's are, an explicit `--title` or `--body` overriding.
   - (tool) Commit the pair, `vc-x1 commit -s b --opening`, the trailers stamped.
   - (tool) Install the dev build again, from the committed tree.
4. Do the next work rung, the head of the loop:
   - (tool) Sync, optional between the bookends.
   - (tool?) Mark the rung `(current)` with its suffix, and bump the version-of-record to it.
   - (hand) Do the work.
   - (hand) Write the rung's subsection, what changed conceptually.
5. Test and review the work rung:
   - (tool) Validate, `--fast` while a review iterates and full before the commit.
   - (tool) Install the dev build.
   - (hand) Test, by the user, the agent, and others, each running the dev build.
   - (hand) Review, and back to step 4 until the user's go.
6. Commit the work rung:
   - (tool?) Flip the marker to `(done)`.
   - (hand) Title and body, the rung's own problem and solution.
   - (tool) Commit the pair, `vc-x1 commit -s b`.
   - (tool) Install the dev build again.
7. Optionally push the rung, a draft on the cycle's bookmark:
   - (hand) The user's approval of this push.
   - (tool) `vc-x1 push -s b`.
8. Loop to step 4 while a rung is left. Unplanned work enters here:
   - (hand) The user picks a rung inserted into the ladder or a `## Todo` entry.
   - (hand) Edits already in `@` are set aside as a jj commit with a local bookmark.
9. Commit the cycle closing:
   - (tool) Sync, and stop when a `main` moved.
   - (hand) Run the acceptance check and record pass or fail.
   - (hand) Finalize the record: the title, the solution as done, the design subsections, the
     closing rung's subsection, and what must outlive the cycle written into `notes/`.
   - (hand) Write the continuation notes.
   - (hand) Update `notes/README.md` when functionality changed.
   - (tool) Record the agent-files' size when one changed, `vc-x1 agent-files size`, its note by
     hand.
   - (hand) Decide the parents: the heads the closing joins, and the target as first parent when
     it is a trapezoid, a linear closing having one parent.
   - (tool?) Mark the closing `(current)` and bump the version-of-record to the bare version.
   - (tool) Validate, full.
   - (hand) Review.
   - (tool?) Flip the marker to `(done)`.
   - (tool) Title and body: read from the opening, " opening" changed to " closing", the body
     from `[closing] body`, when `--title` and `--body` are not given.
   - (tool) Move the block to `## Closed` and make the closing commit, `vc-x1 commit -s b
     --closing <BM|REV> --onto <BOOKMARK>`.
10. Test the cycle:
    - (tool) Validate the closed tree, and install its dev build.
    - (hand) Test, by the user, the agent, and others.
    - (hand) A fault found here goes back to step 4, and the closing is made again.
11. Optionally push the cycle, still a draft on its bookmark:
    - (hand) The user's approval, then (tool) `vc-x1 push -s b`.
12. Land on the target, `main` or another bookmark:
    - (hand) The user's go.
    - (tool) Sync, and stop when the target moved, the closing then made again and tested again.
    - (tool) Commit the agent `@` as the partner of the work commits not yet covered.
    - (tool) Fast-forward the target and delete the cycle's local bookmark, `vc-x1 land -s b
      --onto <BOOKMARK>`.
13. Optionally push the target, which publishes the cycle:
    - (hand) The user's approval, the closing words said first.
    - (tool) `vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark <BOOKMARK>`, or by the user after the session,
      `vc-x1 squash-push -s b`.
    - (tool) Delete the cycle's bookmark on `origin` when it was ever pushed, `vc-x1
      delete-bookmark`.
14. After the Land:
    - (tool) Build, smoke check, and install the release build, `vc-x1 install`.
    - (hand) Stop, and the user restarts the agent.

A dead end leaves the loop at any rung for step 9, its closing `--dead-end`.

What the list raises, each to be decided:

- The way back from step 10: a fault found after the closing has nowhere to go in wink's list. We
  think the closing is made again while it is local, dropped, a rung added, closed and tested
  again, and once pushed a fault is a new rung and a new closing, or a new cycle.
- Step 10 tests what lands only when the Land is a fast-forward. `vc-x1 land` only fast-forwards
  today, and a target that moved means the closing is made again. A linear closing keeps that: it
  is refused when its target moved, never joined at the Land, so no commit lands untested.
- The parents are one decision: "other commits to incorporate" and "the list of parents" are both
  the parent list, each head joined a parent and the target as first parent the trapezoid, which
  is wink's `--closing [REV,...] --trapezoid <T>`.
- The acceptance check and step 10 are two tests: the closing records the check's result, and step
  10 runs after the closing. We think the check runs on the last work rung and the closing records
  it, and step 10 validates the closed tree, which differs from the tip only when the merge
  brought the target's changes in.
- How much of step 1 `vc-x1 open` does: the bookmark today, and the `## Closed` deletion, the
  scaffold, the ladder, and the bump are mechanical and where an agent drifts. Each stays a
  separate operation a user can run or skip, so the flow can be changed.
- Deliberation comes before the opening commit, as in this cycle, so the opening carries the plan.
  The Cycle Protocol says the opening is setup, and is revised to say so.
- One shape or two: wink's list gives every cycle an opening and a closing commit. One shape is the
  easiest to follow, at two commits for a one-line fix. The other way, the opening commit is
  optional and a closing with none above the target carries everything, which is today's
  single-step cycle without its finalize in place, the case that surprised wink in `wt-21-6`.
- Two kinds of push: steps 7 and 11 publish the cycle's bookmark, a draft, and step 13 publishes
  the target and removes the draft. Naming them apart stops one being taken for the other.
- The markers and the bump, at steps 3, 4, 6, and 9: a `(tool?)` each, and we think `commit` does
  the flip, since "done" is true at the commit, and a rung-start command the mark and the bump.
- The opening's title and body default as the closing's do (wink, 2026-11-11): a closing needs no
  `--title` or `--body` when there is an opening, and the opening could need none given the
  bookmark's title.

#### Rungs

The rung subsections, in the ladder's order.

Before going through the questions I'd like to discuss at least one term we use, "land" I believe this is really
ff-merge (fast-forward merge) in jj/git parlance and although to date we've always had ff-merges in the general
case where there are multiple commits merging at once a regular merge is more common.

content.text:
**Land**

You're right about the mechanism: `vc-x1 land` is a fast-forward of the target. I'd still keep two things apart.

- **We already do regular merges, at the closing.** A trapezoid closing is a real merge commit of the target and the ladder. Git's `merge` makes the merge commit and advances the branch in one act. We split those: the closing makes the merge, and land advances the target to it. That split is what lets us test the merged tree before the target moves.
- **Every integration ends in a fast-forward of the target.** Whether the commits were prepared by a merge, a rebase, or nothing, the target bookmark only ever moves forward onto them. So "ff" describes the ref move, and merge or rebase describes how the commits were prepared.

So I'd keep "Land" as the name for the moment a cycle becomes permanent, which is how forges and trunk-based teams use the word, and say plainly that its mechanism is a fast-forward. The general case you describe then becomes "prepare, then advance":

| Prepare | Shape on the target | When the target has moved |
|---|---|---|
| nothing | linear, as committed | refused |
| merge | trapezoid | joined by the merge |
| rebase | linear | ladder replayed on top |

**Rebase**

It fits in two places: mid-cycle, to bring a cycle up to a moved target, and at the closing, as the way a linear shape handles a moved target. Three costs follow from it.

- **Tested commits change.** A rebase rewrites every rung, so the cycle is tested again. The `ochid:` trailers survive, since they are change ids.
- **A pushed draft needs a forced push**, under the usual approval.
- **Our own flow manufactures the conflicts.** Every cycle edits `TODO.md`, `zTOC.md`, and the version in `Cargo.toml`. Two cycles in flight will conflict in all three on any merge or rebase, whatever the code did. We haven't hit it because we run one cycle at a time. I think this is the bigger finding: the record and the version live in shared files, and that will hurt before the choice of merge or rebase does.

**Validate, build, install are not ours**

I agree, and it changes three things in what we just wrote.

- **The Flow needs a fourth mark.** Validate, the dev install, testing, and the release install are the project's work, not cycle management. So is the version bump: I marked it as a candidate for `vc-x1`, but it would put Cargo knowledge into the tool. The ladder markers are ours; the version is theirs.
- **The boundary I'd draw is a hook.** The tool knows that a gate exists at a point in the cycle, not what it runs. It runs a command the project configured and reads the exit status. `validate` is nearly that already, since it only runs lists from the config. What is truly work-specific is build, install, run, profiles, and the dev suffix.
- **The rung I laddered an hour ago is now questionable.** "validate prints only what failed" invests in a command you intend to drop. The Long output rule plus `-q` on the cargo lines in the config gets most of the benefit with no code. I'd drop the rung, unless quiet capture is built as the generic hook runner, which vc-x2 would keep.

For this cycle I'd not remove anything from vc-x1, only stop adding to those commands and design the flow so those steps are pluggable. The rehearsal script helps here: a `~/tmp` workspace with no cargo project is a direct test of "knows nothing about the work".

The plain version: land is a fast-forward and should say so, merge and rebase are two ways to prepare the commits before it, and the tool should run the project's checks as a black box and stop there.

**Question 1: the way back when the test of the closed cycle finds a fault.**

Your list tests after the closing commit, and a fault found there has no next step. There are three ways to handle it.

| Option | What happens | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| A. Reopen | Drop the closing commit, add a fix rung, close again, test again | The closing is made twice |
| B. Fix on top | Add a rung above the closing, then a second closing | History reads closing, fix, closing, and the opening/closing pair no longer brackets the ladder |
| C. Fix inside | Fold the fix into the closing commit | A work change hides inside a bookkeeping merge, and the closing no longer describes only bookkeeping |

I recommend A, for every case before the Land.

- **It is a clean undo for a ladder.** The closing is its own commit and carries all the bookkeeping: the block moved to `## Closed`, the final markers, the bare version. Dropping it puts the tip back exactly as the last rung left it, with the record still in `## In Progress`.
- **A pushed draft does not change the answer.** I earlier suggested a different rule once the closing was pushed, and I now think that was wrong. The cycle's bookmark is a draft until the Land and may be rewritten, so reopening a pushed closing is the same operation plus a forced push, under the usual approval.
- **After the Land it is a new cycle.** The commits are permanent and the record is never amended.
- **A single-step cycle has no closing to drop.** Its fix is folded into its one commit, which `vc-x1 squash` already does.

It needs one tool decision. Today reopening would be `jj abandon` by hand. I'd give it a command, with one of two forms:

- **`--closing` run again replaces an existing closing.** No new command, but a second run silently rewrites a commit.
- **An explicit reopen operation.** One more command, and nothing is replaced without being asked.

I lean to the explicit one, since a closing that silently replaces itself is the kind of surprise this cycle is meant to remove.

Do you agree with A, and which form for the tool?

**Question 2: does the Land ever create a commit?**

Today `vc-x1 land` only fast-forwards. If the destination moved after the closing, it refuses, and the closing has to be made again. The question is whether to keep that or let a Land merge on the spot, as git's `merge` does.

| Option | When the destination has moved | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| A. Fast-forward only | Land refuses and names the ways to prepare again | What was tested is exactly what lands |
| B. Land may merge | Land makes a merge commit and advances to it | One command, but the merged tree lands untested |

I recommend A, with the choice moved to the preparation instead of removed.

- **The refusal offers the choices.** It says the destination moved and names them: close again by merge, rebase the ladder, or whatever else the user decides. That matches your answer to question 1: the tool stops and the user picks.
- **Whether to test again is the user's call.** The tool makes the newly prepared commits testable before the destination moves. It does not insist on a test.
- **One command stays possible by composition.** `commit --closing ... --land` already prepares and advances in one invocation, for a user who wants git's behaviour and accepts the risk. So B's convenience exists without `land` itself ever making a commit.
- **It keeps one meaning for the word.** "Land advances a bookmark to commits that already exist" is true in every case: linear, trapezoid, rebased, any destination.

Do you agree that `land` itself stays fast-forward only, with merge and rebase as preparations the user chooses?

**Question 4: the acceptance check and the test of the closed cycle.**

The closing commit records whether the acceptance check passed, but your list tests the cycle after the closing commit. So the result is written before the test it reports. There are three ways to order them.

| Option | When the acceptance check runs | What the test after the closing is |
|---|---|---|
| A. Two tests | On the last work rung, before the closing, which records it | A separate check of the closed tree |
| B. One test, recorded later | After the closing | The acceptance check itself, with its result recorded by amending the closing or in a later commit |
| C. One test, not recorded in the tree | After the closing | The acceptance check, with its result recorded outside the commits |

I recommend A as the default, with the user free to do otherwise.

- **The closing adds no work.** In a linear closing, or a trapezoid whose destination has not moved, the closed tree differs from the last rung's only in bookkeeping. A check that passed on the last rung is still true.
- **The second test earns its place when a merge or rebase brought in changes.** Then the closed tree is new, and the test after the closing is the only one that has seen it.
- **B rewrites the closing after testing it**, so the commit that lands is not the commit that was tested. That is the problem the Land's fast-forward default exists to avoid.
- **C fits your "the work is not ours" direction** if the result belongs to the project and not the cycle's record. It loses the record of pass or fail in the landmark commit, which today is the only place a reader finds it.

A side effect of A is that the two tests want different names, so the protocol can tell them apart. "Acceptance check" stays for the first. The second needs one: "closed-tree test" is accurate but clumsy.

Do you agree with A as the default, and do you have a name for the second test?

**Question 5: how much of opening a cycle does `vc-x1 open` do?**

Today `open` only creates the bookmark. Four more sub-steps of opening are mechanical and done by hand. I did all four by hand an hour ago, two of them by deleting line ranges by number, which is exactly where a slip happens.

| Sub-step | Whose it is | My view |
|---|---|---|
| Delete what `## Closed` holds | The cycle's record | `open` does it |
| Move the Todo entry into an In Progress scaffold | The cycle's record | `open` does it |
| Replace the ladder in `zTOC.md` with opening and closing | The cycle's record | `open` does it |
| Bump the version in `Cargo.toml` | The project's work | Not `open`: a hook, or by hand |

I recommend `open` does the first three and leaves the version alone.

- **The record is cycle management.** `TODO.md` and `zTOC.md` have a shape the agent-files define, so the tool can know it without knowing anything about the work.
- **The version is the project's.** This follows your "the work is not ours" point: bumping it in the tool means knowing Cargo.
- **Each part stays skippable.** A project with no `TODO.md`, or one that keeps its record elsewhere, runs `open` for the bookmark alone. I'd make the record steps the default when the files are present and let a flag turn them off, so nothing fails on a workspace that lacks them.
- **Choosing the entry stays by hand.** `open --title` would look for a `## Todo` entry with that title and move it. If none matches, it writes an empty scaffold under the title.

content.text:
Yes, an xtask can do it, and the comment problem is solved.

**Comments survive with `toml_edit`.** You're right that the usual `toml` crate parses into plain data and loses comments and layout when it writes back. `toml_edit` is built for the opposite: it keeps every comment, blank line, and key order, and changes only the value you set. Cargo itself uses it for `cargo add`. It is already in our build as a dependency of jj-lib, though not one we declare directly, so an xtask using it adds no new download.

**Two smaller points on the mechanics:**

- **`Cargo.lock` has to follow.** Our build runs with `--locked`, so a stale lock file fails it. The xtask should refresh the lock in the same step. The lock updated on its own during validation today only because the test run is not `--locked`.
- **A simpler fallback exists.** For one known line, `version = "..."` under `[package]`, a targeted text replacement also preserves everything and needs no library. It is more fragile, and I'd only use it if we wanted the xtask to have zero dependencies.

**The split I'd propose between the tool and the project:**

- **The tool computes the version, because the suffix scheme is cycle knowledge.** `-0` at the opening, `-1`, `-2` for the rungs, and bare at the closing are rules of the cycle, not of Rust.
- **The project reads and writes it.** Two commands in `.vc-config.md`, one that prints the current version and one that sets a given version. For us both would be xtask calls. A Python project would point them at its own script.
- **With neither configured, the bump stays by hand** and the tool says so.

That keeps the tool ignorant of Cargo while still automating the step, and it is the same hook boundary as for validation: the tool knows a version exists and when it changes, not where it is stored.

**Costs:** an xtask crate turns the repo into a Cargo workspace, which touches the build layout. There is already a Todo for it, **Build config moves to an xtask**, so the bump could be that xtask's first job.

The plain version: `toml_edit` keeps comments, the tool decides what the next version is, and a small xtask writes it.

Shall I record this as the decision for the version bump, with the xtask as a candidate rung?

content.text:
Recorded, in three parts:

- **`open` does the three record steps by default.**
- **The tool never bumps the version, now or later.** I noted that this replaces my split, where the tool computed the version and a hook wrote it, since that was still the tool doing the bump.
- **The project automates its own bump.** Ours is an xtask using `toml_edit`, listed as a candidate rung.

Your check, refusing a commit whose version did not change, is recorded as your idea with two points left to decide. My thoughts on each:

**How the tool sees the change**

| Option | How it works | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| A. A `version.md` file | The tool checks whether that file changed in the commit | Simple and language-neutral, but the version then lives in two places, `version.md` and `Cargo.toml`, and something must keep them equal |
| B. A file and a pattern in the config | The config names `Cargo.toml` and the line `version = `; the tool checks whether a matching line is in the commit's diff | No second copy; the tool still knows nothing about Cargo, only a path and a pattern |
| C. A list of files that must change | The config names files every rung must touch | Simplest, but any edit to `Cargo.toml` passes, such as adding a dependency |

I'd pick B. Cargo requires the version in `Cargo.toml`, so with A the xtask would write both files, and the check would be on the copy, not the real one. A is the right answer for a project with no manifest at all, and B covers that case too by pointing at whatever file the project uses, `version.md` included.

**The flag**

I'd not reuse `--yes`. On `push` it means "the user approved this forced push", and the rules note an agent can type it as easily as anything else. A second meaning on `commit` makes it a general "skip the question" switch. A flag that names what is being waived, something like `--same-version`, keeps each waiver specific and visible in the command.

**One scope note:** the check applies to the work-repo commit only. The agent-repo has no version.

Which do you prefer for seeing the change, and are you fine with a named flag instead of `--yes`?

**Question 6: is the deliberation part of opening, before the opening commit?**

The Cycle Protocol today describes the opening commit as setup: bookmark, record moved, version bumped. The plan is expected to grow afterwards, revised as rungs land. In this cycle we did it your way instead: opened, then deliberated, and the opening commit will carry the plan.

| Option | What the opening commit holds | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| A. Deliberate first | The problem, solution, acceptance check, decisions, and the planned ladder | The opening is a real review point, but the bookmark can sit uncommitted for hours while we talk |
| B. Commit the setup, then deliberate | Only the scaffold | Quick and mechanical, but the plan arrives in a later rung and the opening review has nothing to review |
| C. The user decides per cycle | Either | No rule to follow, and a small cycle skips deliberation entirely |

I recommend A as the default and C as the stated freedom.

- **The opening review becomes meaningful.** Reviewing a scaffold is a formality. Reviewing the plan before any work is where a wrong direction is cheapest to catch.
- **The plan stays provisional.** Committing it does not freeze it. Later rungs still revise the record, as the protocol already allows.
- **The long uncommitted stretch is a real cost.** Everything we have written today is only in the working copy. Your Todo **Work in progress is durable and continues on any machine** is about exactly this gap. Until that exists, the mitigation is that the opening can be committed as soon as the plan is good enough to start, not when it is perfect.
- **A small cycle needs no deliberation.** Its record can say `_None._` under Deliberation, which the format already permits, so A costs it nothing.

If you agree, the protocol's Opening section gets a deliberation step between the scaffold and the commit, and its description of the opening as "setup" is changed.

Do you agree with A as the default, with the user free to commit the setup first?

**Question 7: does every cycle have an opening commit and a closing commit?**

Your list gives every cycle both. Today a small change can be a single-step cycle: one commit carrying the opening's duties, the work, and the closing's duties. There are two ways to reach it today, and one of them is what surprised you in `wt-21-6`.

| Option | A one-line fix is | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| A. One shape, always | Three commits: opening, the work, closing | One flow to learn, but heavy for small changes, and the history fills with bookkeeping commits |
| B. Opening optional, closing always | One commit, when no opening was committed: the closing carries everything | Two shapes, but each decided by a plain fact: was an opening committed or not |
| C. As today | One commit, reached two ways, including finalizing a committed opening in place | The in-place case rewrites a commit and is the one that surprised you |

I recommend B.

- **It drops the surprising case and keeps the cheap one.** A closing never rewrites an existing commit. If an opening was committed, the closing is a new commit above it, even when there is no work rung between.
- **The rule is one sentence.** A closing is always a new commit. With nothing committed above the destination, it is the cycle's only commit.
- **Shape still follows from the commit count**, as the protocol says now, so nothing has to be chosen up front. A user who starts small and finds the work growing commits an opening and carries on.
- **It fits question 6.** A cycle worth deliberating commits its opening with the plan. A cycle too small to deliberate skips the opening commit and closes in one.

Two consequences to accept:

- **A cycle with a committed opening and no work rung becomes two commits**, opening and closing, where today it collapses to one. That is rare and honest: it is what was actually done.
- **`open` still runs for a single commit cycle**, since it makes the bookmark and now the record scaffold. Only the opening commit is skipped.

Do you agree with B?

Recorded: every cycle has an opening and a closing, and in a single-step cycle the closing is squashed into the opening, with the title losing its trailing word. The tool tells the two shapes apart and handles `--title` and `--body` given or not.

A correction on my side: I said finalizing in place was the case that surprised you in `wt-21-6`. Nothing in the record says that, and I should not have claimed it. I noted the error in the record.

One detail I recorded as my reading for you to confirm: the tool tells the shapes apart by the commit count, as the protocol says now.

- No commit, or only the opening, above the destination: single-step. Any work still in the working copy is folded into that one commit.
- More than one commit: a ladder, and its closing is a separate commit titled with " closing".

**Question 8: the pushes are of two kinds and need two names.**

Your list has three optional pushes. Two of them do one thing and the third does another.

| Push | What it publishes | Reversible? |
|---|---|---|
| After a rung, and after the closing | The cycle's own bookmark | Yes: it is a draft and may still be rewritten, with a forced push |
| After the Land | The destination bookmark, and it removes the cycle's bookmark from the remote | No: the commits are permanent |

The protocol calls all three "push", and the approval rule treats them alike. I think that hides the difference that matters most, which is whether the push can be taken back.

I recommend naming them apart in the protocol, and keeping one command.

- **Names:** "draft push" for the first kind and "publish" for the second. The second already has a word in the protocol's Land sequence, "Publish", so only "draft push" is new.
- **One command, `vc-x1 push`, for both.** The bookmark it is given already says which kind it is. A second command would add surface without adding a choice.
- **The approval rule stays per push**, for both kinds. What changes is that a waiver has to say which kind it covers. The rules already ask for this: a waiver over a cycle's pushes must say whether the Land is inside it.
- **The tool can say which kind it is doing.** `push` prints whether the bookmark is a cycle's draft or a destination, so the user approving it sees what they are approving.

Do you agree with the two names and the single command?

I think a `cycle` command is the right direction, and I'd adjust its form in three ways.

**Why it's right**

- **`commit` does too many jobs.** It makes a plain rung, an opening, a closing that may be a merge or a rewrite in place, moves the record, lands, pushes, and describes an older commit. Most of the flow's surprises sit in how those flags combine.
- **It gives the cycle one home.** Everything that knows about cycles moves under one word, and `commit` goes back to meaning "commit the pair with trailers". It also gives "where does this cycle stand and what comes next" a natural place, which an older Todo of yours asks for.
- **It names the two pushes for free.** A push of the cycle's bookmark is the draft push, and a push as part of the land is the publish. Question 8 answers itself.

**What I'd change**

1. **Subcommands, not flags: `cycle open`, `cycle close`, `cycle land`.** Flags that are mutually exclusive verbs are subcommands in disguise. As flags, every combination like `--open --closing` has to be refused by hand, and each verb's options show up in one long help. As subcommands, the closing's parent list belongs only to `close`.

2. **Keep composition as "this stage and onward".** The one thing flags do better is chaining, such as closing, landing, and pushing in one invocation. The stages have a fixed order, so `cycle close --land --push` covers it without making the verbs themselves flags.

3. **Drop the separate "opening" verb.** `--open` and `--opening` differ by three letters and mean different things: one makes the bookmark and scaffold, the other commits. An agent will mix them up. The tool can tell that a commit is the cycle's first, so the first commit on a cycle is the opening without being told. This is the same "the tool knows" principle you applied to single-step cycles.

That leaves four verbs plus a status:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cycle open` | Bookmark and record scaffold |
| `cycle commit` | A rung; the first one is the opening |
| `cycle close` | The closing, or the squash into the opening for a single-step cycle |
| `cycle land` | Advance the destination, fast-forward by default |
| `cycle status` | Where the cycle stands and what may come next |

**The cost, and a choice it forces**

This is a large rename late in vc-x1's life, and your Todo list already has it as vc-x2's: **vc-x2: a cycle command, open, close, and land**. Two spellings for the same act is worse than either one alone. So I see two honest options:

- **Do it in this cycle and remove the old forms in the same cycle.** The rehearsal script is then written once, against the final names.
- **Leave it to vc-x2.** This cycle fixes behaviour under today's names, and the protocol text is written so the rename is mechanical later.

I lean to doing it here. The flow is what this cycle is about, the rehearsal would otherwise be rewritten, and the protocol we are about to revise would be revised twice.

The plain version: yes to `cycle`, as subcommands, with the opening inferred instead of named, and either do the rename fully now or not at all.

Recorded: the `cycle` command as your proposal, with my thoughts beside it and nothing marked decided. That includes the form (subcommands or flags), the inferred opening, and whether it is done here or left to vc-x2.

**Question 9: who sets the ladder's markers?**

Each rung in `zTOC.md` is marked `(current)` when it starts and `(done)` when it is committed. Both edits are by hand today, at four points in the flow, and they are easy to forget because nothing fails when one is missed.

| Marker | When it is true | Who could set it |
|---|---|---|
| `(done)` | The moment the rung is committed | The commit itself |
| `(current)` | When work on the rung starts | Nothing in the tool marks that moment today |

I recommend the tool sets both, at the commit.

- **`(done)` belongs to the commit.** It is true exactly when the commit is made, so the command that commits the rung flips it. The rung is found by its title, which the commit already has, since the ladder entry and the commit title are identical by rule.
- **`(current)` moves to the next rung at the same commit.** When a rung is committed, the next unmarked rung in the ladder becomes current. That needs no new command for "starting a rung", and the ladder always shows where the cycle stands.
- **The version suffix on the rung is the one gap.** A rung's line also shows its version suffix, such as `- 2 (done)`. We decided the tool never bumps the version, so it cannot invent that number. It can read it from the same file and pattern the version check uses, and leave it blank when no such key is configured.
- **The edits are part of the rung's own commit.** The marker change is in the working copy before the commit is made, so it lands in the commit it describes.

One consequence: if the ladder has no rung with the commit's title, the tool has to choose between refusing and committing without marking. I'd have it say so and commit anyway. Unplanned rungs are common, and a refusal there would push people to edit the ladder just to satisfy the tool.

Do you agree that the commit flips `(done)` and advances `(current)`, and that a title not in the ladder is reported but not refused?

I think it's a good idea, with one real loss and one gain larger than the syntax.

**For it**

- **The pattern already exists.** `.vc-config.md` is markdown with `toml` blocks that the tool parses, so both the format and the parser are in place.
- **Reads and writes become exact.** The tool sets a field on a rung instead of pattern-matching a markdown line, and `toml_edit` keeps comments and layout when it writes.
- **It can hold more than the ladder.** This is the larger gain. The tool needs to know the cycle's title, its bookmark, and its destination. One open candidate in our list is "`open` records the cycle's bookmark, and commit advances that one alone". A `toml` block is where that record would live, so the ladder section becomes the cycle's machine-readable state.

**Against it**

- **The links go.** Today each rung is a markdown link that opens its subsection in `TODO.md`. Inside a code block nothing is clickable. The anchor can be derived from the title, so the tool can print the links in a status command, but a person reading `zTOC.md` in a preview loses the click.
- **It can get tall.** Written as one table per rung it is four lines each. Written as one inline table per line it stays as compact as today.

A shape that keeps one line per rung:

```toml
[cycle]
title = "feat: improve vc-x1 cycle flow"
bookmark = "feat-improve-vc-x1-cycle-flow"
destination = "main"

rungs = [
  { state = "done",    title = "feat: improve vc-x1 cycle flow opening" },
  { state = "current", title = "feat: validate prints only what failed" },
  { state = "",        title = "feat: improve vc-x1 cycle flow closing" },
]
```

Two things fall out of this shape:

- **The version suffix can leave the ladder.** It is the project's, not the cycle's, and the tool would otherwise have to read it from the manifest to fill it in.
- **The alternative is a strict grammar for the markdown line.** Today's line is already regular, one rung per line, so the tool could parse and validate it as is and keep the links. That is less formal and has nowhere to put the bookmark and destination.

I'd choose the `toml` block, mainly for the cycle state it can hold, and accept the lost links.

The plain version: yes, make it `toml`, because the tool then has one defined place for both the ladder and the facts about the cycle it currently has to guess.

Shall I record the tool managing the markers as decided, and the `toml` ladder as the form, or do you want the links kept?

I think the planning stays with a person or the agent, and the tool should do the copying.

**The split I'd make**

- **Deciding the rungs is judgment.** What the rungs are, their titles, and their order come out of the deliberation. No tool should guess that.
- **Writing them in two places is mechanical.** Today each rung is typed twice: a line in `zTOC.md` and a subsection heading under `#### Rungs` in `TODO.md`. The title must match exactly or the link breaks, and nothing catches it. That is the part the tool should take.

**How**

Make the rung subsection headings in `TODO.md` the one place a rung is written. A rung needs its subsection anyway, since that is where its intent goes. The tool then builds the ladder in `zTOC.md` from those headings: one line per heading, in the same order, with the link computed from the title. `open` already computes that same slug to name the bookmark.

Adding, dropping, or reordering a rung is then one edit in `TODO.md`, and the ladder follows.

**A further step: the markers need not be stored at all**

- A rung is `(done)` when a commit with its title exists on the cycle's branch.
- The `(current)` rung is the first one without such a commit.
- The number is its position.

So the whole ladder can be regenerated from two things the tool can read: the headings and the history. Nothing is flipped by hand and nothing can be forgotten. The tool would rewrite the ladder as part of each cycle commit, so `zTOC.md` in every commit shows the state as of that commit, and you keep the clickable list.

**Where this needs care**

- **A renamed rung.** If a committed rung's heading is later retitled, the title no longer matches its commit and it would read as not done. The rules already say a committed rung keeps its title, so the tool should report the mismatch instead of silently unmarking it.
- **A single-step cycle** has no rung subsections, so its ladder is the one unlinked line with the cycle title, as now.
- **`open` writes the first two headings**, the opening and the closing, so the ladder exists from the start.

The plain version: you write each rung once, as a heading in `TODO.md`, and the tool produces and maintains the clickable ladder from those headings and the commits.

Does that match what you had in mind, or do you want the ladder to remain something we write directly?

Not quite; that is a simpler scheme than the one I described, and it is a fair alternative.

**What I proposed:** the file still shows `(done)` and `(current)` on the lines, exactly as it looks today. The difference is only who writes them. The tool works each marker out from the commits and writes it, so nobody types or flips one.

**What you describe:** only `(current)` is written, and position carries the rest. Everything above it is done, everything below is not.

| | Markers written, computed by the tool | Only `(current)` written |
|---|---|---|
| Reads at a glance | Each line says its own state | You find `(current)` and infer the rest |
| Rungs done out of order | Shown correctly, each line marked by its own commit | Cannot be shown; the line has to be moved first |
| A finished cycle | Every line reads `(done)` | No line has a marker, the same as a ladder not yet started |
| Editing by hand, if the tool is not used | Two markers to keep right | One marker to move |

I'd keep `(done)` written, for two reasons.

- **It costs nothing once the tool writes it.** The argument for leaving it out is fewer things to maintain by hand, and that work is gone either way.
- **Position alone is ambiguous at both ends.** A ladder with no `(current)` could be one that has not started or one that is finished. The finished ladder is the one kept in the landmark commit, so it should say plainly that every rung was done.

Your reading does hold as a rule about a normal ladder: rungs above `(current)` are done and rungs below are not. I'd have the tool report it when that is not so, since a done rung below the current one means the work went out of the planned order and the ladder should probably be reordered to match.

Recorded, including your two points: the naming is now a coding requirement, and the tool errors if any commit in the cycle has no matching rung in `TODO.md`.

That last one replaces what I proposed earlier, where a title missing from the ladder was reported and committed anyway. Two consequences I noted in the record:

- **An unplanned rung gets its heading in `TODO.md` before its commit.**
- **A local ladder needs checking.** Its intermediate commits sit on the cycle's branch until they collapse into the rung, and they would fail the match while they exist.

Two points in that entry are still open: whether the rung's number is its position, and where the cycle's destination is kept.

**Question 10: do the opening's title and body default, as the closing's do?**

Your answer to question 7 mostly settled this: the user gives `--title`, `--body`, both, or neither, and the tool does the right thing. I'd like to confirm the defaults so the record states them.

| Commit | Default title | Default body |
|---|---|---|
| Opening | The cycle title plus " opening" | A configured line, such as "Opens the cycle ...", like the closing's `[closing] body` |
| Closing of a ladder | The cycle title plus " closing" | `[closing] body`, as today |
| Single-step cycle's one commit | The bare cycle title | Needs a real body, since this commit holds the work |
| A work rung | None: it must be given | None: it must be given |

Two details behind the table:

- **The cycle title comes from the `### ` heading under `## In Progress`**, which `open` writes. Today the closing reads it from the opening commit's title. Reading it from the record works for a single-step cycle too, where no opening commit may exist.
- **The single-step body is the one place a default would be wrong.** A pointer body such as "Closes the cycle ..." says nothing about the change. I'd have the tool require `--body` there, or the user's named waiver, and not fill in a bookkeeping line.

Do you agree with those defaults, including requiring a body for the single-step commit?

content.text:
Recorded: the opening and a ladder's closing default their title and body, a single-step commit defaults its title and requires a body, and a work rung requires both.

That was the last of the ten questions. What remains open is from the later discussion:

1. The `cycle` command: its form, and whether it is built here or left to vc-x2.
2. Rebase: where it is offered and under what name.
3. The validate rung: dropped, or rebuilt as a generic hook runner.
4. The flow's own conflicts in `TODO.md`, `zTOC.md`, and the version.
5. Three small points: the rung number, where the destination is kept, and the commit-count test for a single-step cycle.

I'll take them in that order, since the first decides how much this cycle builds.

**Question 11: the `cycle` command.**

You proposed `cycle --open`, `cycle --opening`, `cycle --closing`, and `cycle --land`. I gave thoughts and nothing was decided. There are three separate decisions.

**a. Flags or subcommands**

| Form | Example | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Flags, as you proposed | `cycle --closing --land --push` | Stages chain naturally, but exclusive combinations must be refused by hand and all options share one help |
| Subcommands | `cycle close --land --push` | Each stage has its own options and help, and chaining is kept as "this stage and onward" |

I recommend subcommands.

**b. Is the opening named or inferred**

| Form | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| Named: an `--opening` beside `--open` | Explicit, but the two words are three letters apart and mean different acts |
| Inferred: the first commit of a cycle is its opening | One less thing to say, and consistent with the tool knowing a single-step cycle |

I recommend inferred. The verbs would be `open`, `commit`, `close`, `land`, and `status`.

**c. Here or vc-x2**

| Choice | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| Here, with the old `commit --opening`, `--closing`, `--land` forms removed in this cycle | The largest piece of work in the ladder, but the rehearsal and the protocol are written once, against the final names |
| vc-x2 | This cycle stays smaller and fixes behaviour under today's names; the rehearsal and protocol are revised again later |

I recommend here. Nearly every decision we have recorded today changes `open`, the commit, or the closing. Making those changes under the old names and renaming afterwards is doing the work twice.

How do you want to decide a, b, and c?

message.content:
I like your recommendations, one tiny issue, we previously changed from sometimes having `commands subcommands` to always
having only `commands --options|-o` as it was consistent. For vc-x1 I think we should stick with "no subcommands". But in
vc-x2 we'll reevaluate that decision.

Thoughts only.

content.text:
Sticking with "no subcommands" for vc-x1 is the right call. A consistent command shape is worth more than the tidier help I was after, and mixing shapes late in vc-x1 would be its own inconsistency. Here is how my recommendations change.

**Decision a becomes: mode flags on `cycle`**

- **The flags would be `--open`, `--commit`, `--close`, `--land`, and `--status`.** That is your original proposal with my change from decision b: no `--opening`, because the first commit of a cycle is inferred to be its opening.
- **My objection to flags was weaker than I made it sound.** I said exclusive combinations would have to be refused by hand. The argument parser we use can declare that a group of flags excludes each other, and that an option is only valid with a given flag, so those refusals are declared, not hand-written.
- **Chaining works as you first wrote it.** `cycle --close --land --push` runs the stages in their fixed order. The parser only has to allow the combinations that are consecutive stages.
- **Stage flags can carry their own value.** `--close` takes the list of heads joined, and `--land` takes the destination, as in your earlier closing design.
- **The one cost that stays is a long help.** All stages share one help text. Grouping the options under a heading per stage keeps it readable.

**It ports to vc-x2 cleanly.** If vc-x2 decides for subcommands, `cycle --close` becomes `cycle close` and nothing else moves. The names and the behaviour are settled here either way.

**What happens to the existing commands**

- **`open` and `land` are removed** in the same cycle, replaced by `cycle --open` and `cycle --land`. Keeping both spellings is what we agreed to avoid.
- **`commit` loses `--opening`, `--closing`, and `--land`** and stays as the plain commit of the pair with its trailers, for work outside a cycle.

**One inconsistency I noticed while reading the agent-files:** `vc-x1 agent-files copy --from`, `agent-files diff`, and `agent-files size` are a command with subcommands today. If the rule is "no subcommands", those are an exception still standing. It does not affect this decision, and I mention it only so it is not a surprise later.

The plain version: `cycle` with mode flags instead of subcommands, the opening inferred, the old spellings removed here, and vc-x2 free to turn the flags into subcommands.

Recorded as decided: `cycle` with mode flags, the opening inferred, built in this cycle with `open`, `land`, and the cycle flags on `commit` removed.

**Question 12: where is rebase offered?**

You said rebase is an operation we should support. We recorded two places it fits and its costs, but not whether the tool does it or under what name.

| Place | What it does | Without tool support |
|---|---|---|
| Mid-cycle | Moves the cycle's commits onto a destination that has moved | `jj rebase` by hand |
| At the close | Gives a linear result on a destination that has moved, with no merge commit | `jj rebase` by hand, then close |

There are three levels of support.

| Option | What the tool does | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| A. Nothing | The protocol says when a rebase is appropriate, and it is done with `jj` | No code, but it breaks "the tool is the interface", and nothing checks the result |
| B. One mode flag, `cycle --rebase <DEST>` | Rebases the cycle's commits onto the destination, usable at any point before the land | One operation serves both places |
| C. A shape on the close | `cycle --close` takes a shape: merge or rebase | Rebase is only reachable at the close, so the mid-cycle case stays by hand |

I recommend B.

- **One operation covers both places.** Rebasing at the close is just rebasing and then closing, and the two chain: `cycle --rebase main --close`.
- **The tool can do what a hand rebase skips.** It can refuse when the cycle's bookmark was pushed, unless the user asks, since that needs a forced push. It can report conflicts and stop. It can say that the rebased commits are new and were not tested.
- **The links survive.** The `ochid:` trailers are change ids, which a rebase keeps, so the agent-repo side needs no rewrite.
- **It completes the picture for a moved destination.** The Land's refusal can then name all three ways on, each a real command: merge at the land, close again as a merge, or rebase.

Two costs to accept:

- **Our own files will conflict.** A rebase replays every rung, and each one edits `TODO.md`, `zTOC.md`, and the version. Against a destination where another cycle has landed, each rung may conflict. That is the conflict problem in question 14, and rebase is where it bites hardest.
- **It is more work in a cycle that is already large.** If the ladder gets too long, this is the piece I would defer first, since we have never needed it in practice.

Do you want B, and should it be built in this cycle or filed as a Todo?

**Question 13: what happens to the validate rung?**

Earlier today we laddered **feat: validate prints only what failed** as the first work rung. Then you decided that validate, test, build, run, and install are the project's work and will not be in vc-x2. So the rung improves a command that is going away.

| Option | What is done | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| A. Drop the rung, quiet cargo in the config | Add `-q` to the `cargo clippy` and `cargo test` lines in `.vc-config.md` | No code, and the Long output rule covers the rest; `validate` itself is unchanged |
| B. Keep the rung as planned | `validate` captures output and prints only failures | Fixes it for every user of vc-x1, but invests in a command with no future |
| C. Build it as a generic runner | A small piece that runs a configured command, captures its output, and reports pass or fail | Reusable by vc-x2 as the hook boundary, but it is design work for vc-x2 done inside vc-x1 |

I recommend A.

- **The problem is already contained.** The Long output rule kept the full output in a file and showed the tail for every run since we added it, and no run has been repeated.
- **`-q` removes most of the noise at the source.** Cargo then prints no `Compiling` lines, and each test becomes a dot instead of a line. A failure still prints in full.
- **The ladder is already large.** The `cycle` command, the record steps in `open`, the computed ladder, the version check, and the rehearsal are all in this cycle. Spending a rung on a command due for removal is the easiest thing to cut.
- **C is the right idea in the wrong place.** How vc-x2 runs a project's checks is a design question for vc-x2, with its own decisions about hooks and exit codes.

One consequence of A: `-q` changes what you see at your own terminal as well, since the config is shared. If you prefer the full output when you run validation yourself, the alternative is to leave the config alone and rely on the Long output rule only.

Do you agree with A, and do you want `-q` in the config or the config left as it is?

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

Solution: a loader finds and reads the file and a parser takes text and
returns the schema, so a test hands the parser a string, and `main` gets
the schema from one call. See details in TODO.md.
```

The second opens "Solution:" and ends with the pointer, and nothing names a file that the diff
already lists.

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". See details in
TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body names the cycle by its title and points at
its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".
