tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# cycle-rehearsal.sh - run the cycle flow end to end, by `cycle`'s flags.
#
# Makes a throwaway dual workspace with local bare remotes and no cargo
# project, and runs three cycles through it, open to Land, checking
# what each command left:
#
#   1. a single-step cycle with nothing committed before its closing
#   2. a single-step cycle whose opening is committed first
#   3. a ladder, closed as a trapezoid, with each way back from a fault
#      found after the closing tried: fix inside, fix on top, reopen
#
# Usage: scripts/cycle-rehearsal.sh [DIR]
#   DIR  where the workspace and its remotes go, removed first
#        [default: ~/tmp/cycle-rehearsal]
#   VC   the binary under test [default: vc-x1-dev]
#
# Exits zero when every check passed. The ways back the tool refuses
# are reported, not failed: the rehearsal's job there is to say which.

set -uo pipefail

VC=${VC:-vc-x1-dev}
ROOT=${1:-$HOME/tmp/cycle-rehearsal}
WS=$ROOT/ws
AGENT=$WS/.agent-session
LOG=$ROOT/rehearsal.log
LINK=$HOME/.claude/projects/$(printf '%s' "$WS" | tr '/.' '--')

checks=0
failed=0
refused=()

say() { printf '%s\n' "$*"; }
step() { say; say "== $*"; }

# Run a command that must succeed, its output kept in the log.
run() {
    say "  \$ $*" | tee -a "$LOG"
    if ! "$@" >>"$LOG" 2>&1; then
        say "  FAILED (exit $?): $*, see $LOG"
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        return 1
    fi
}

# Run a command that is expected to be refused, and say which way it went.
tries() {
    local what=$1
    shift
    say "  \$ $*" | tee -a "$LOG"
    if "$@" >>"$LOG" 2>&1; then
        say "  done: $what"
    else
        say "  refused: $what"
        refused+=("$what")
    fi
}

# check <what> <actual> <expected>
check() {
    checks=$((checks + 1))
    if [ "$2" = "$3" ]; then
        say "  ok: $1"
    else
        say "  NOT OK: $1"
        say "    expected: $3"
        say "    actual:   $2"
        failed=$((failed + 1))
    fi
}

# check_has <what> <text> <fragment>
check_has() {
    checks=$((checks + 1))
    case "$2" in
    *"$3"*) say "  ok: $1" ;;
    *)
        say "  NOT OK: $1"
        say "    missing: $3"
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        ;;
    esac
}

jjw() { jj --ignore-working-copy -R "$WS" "$@"; }
jja() { jj --ignore-working-copy -R "$AGENT" "$@"; }
title() { jjw log -r "$1" --no-graph -T 'description.first_line()'; }
cid() { jjw log -r "$1" --no-graph -T 'commit_id'; }
agent_cid() { jja log -r "$1" --no-graph -T 'commit_id'; }
bookmarks() { jjw bookmark list -T 'name ++ "\n"' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' '; }
remote_bookmarks() {
    git -C "$ROOT/remotes/ws.git" for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads | tr '\n' ' '
}
above_main() { jjw log -r "$1..$2" --no-graph --reversed -T 'description.first_line() ++ "\n"'; }
nparents() { jjw log -r "$1" --no-graph -T 'parents.len()'; }
ladder() { sed -n '/^## Ladder$/,/^## The TOC$/p' "$WS/zTOC.md" | grep '^- '; }

# What every Land leaves: the destination published in both repos, the
# cycle's bookmark gone from both sides, the record closed, and the
# work repo clean.
check_landed() {
    local name=$1 slug=$2
    check "$name: main is published" "$(cid main)" "$(cid main@origin)"
    check "$name: the agent main is published" "$(agent_cid main)" "$(agent_cid main@origin)"
    check "$name: only main is left locally" "$(bookmarks)" "main "
    check "$name: only main is left on origin" "$(remote_bookmarks)" "main "
    check_has "$name: nothing is in progress" "$(cat "$WS/TODO.md")" \
        "_No cycle currently in progress._"
    check "$name: the work @ is empty" "$(jj -R "$WS" log -r @ --no-graph -T 'empty')" "true"
    check_has "$name: the landed commit names its partner" \
        "$(jjw log -r main --no-graph -T description)" "ochid: "
    : "$slug"
}

step "Workspace: $WS, with $VC"
if [ -L "$LINK" ]; then rm "$LINK"; fi
rm -rf "$ROOT"
mkdir -p "$ROOT"
: >"$LOG"
run "$VC" init --target "$WS" --test-repo "$ROOT/remotes" || exit 1

import re,sys
def remove_item(text, sig, indent=''):
    """Remove the item whose signature line starts with indent+sig, with its doc comment and attributes."""
    lines=text.split('\n')
    idx=[i for i,l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith(indent+sig)]
    assert len(idx)==1, (sig, len(idx))
    i=idx[0]
    s=i
    while s>0 and (lines[s-1].startswith(indent+'///') or lines[s-1].startswith(indent+'#[')):
        s-=1
    # multi-line attribute blocks: walk up while previous line is part of #[ ... ] block
    e=i
    if lines[i].rstrip().endswith(';'):
        pass
    else:
        while not (lines[e]==indent+'}' or lines[e].startswith(indent+'}') and lines[e].rstrip() in (indent+'}',indent+'};')):
            e+=1
    # drop one following blank line
    if e+1<len(lines) and lines[e+1]=='':
        e+=1
    del lines[s:e+1]
    return '\n'.join(lines)
EOF

# ---- Cycle shape
section("### Cycle shape\n","### Unplanned work\n",'''### Cycle shape

A cycle's shape is its branch's commit count, so nothing has to be decided before its first commit
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#cycle-shape)). Every cycle has an opening and a closing, and the
count says whether they are one commit.

- Every cycle starts with `vc-x1 cycle --open`, which makes its bookmark on the work `@` and
  writes its record, a single-step cycle included. A cycle's first commit, by `cycle --commit`, is
  its opening, which the tool sees and no flag says.
- No commit on the branch, the work in `@`, is single-step: `cycle --close --body "..."` commits
  `@` as its one commit, under the bare cycle title, and it carries the opening's duties, the work,
  and the close-out's duties.
- One commit, an opening committed first, is single-step too: `cycle --close` squashes the closing
  into it, `@` folded in, the title losing " opening" and gaining no " closing".
- More commits are a ladder: `cycle --close` makes the closing commit, from the work `@` on the
  cycle's tip. `--trapezoid <target>` makes it the merge of the target and the tip, each revision
  listed, `cycle --close <REV,...>`, is another head joined, and `--land <target>` lands it in the
  same invocation.
- A ladder lands as a trapezoid, never squashed: every rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, and a
  squash discards all but one. Without `--trapezoid` the closing is linear, a plain commit on the
  ladder, which is the user's to ask for.
- The titles and bodies default. The opening's is the cycle title plus " opening" and `[opening]
  body`, a ladder's closing the title plus " closing" and `[closing] body`, and a single-step
  cycle's one commit gives its `--body`, since it holds the work. A work rung gives both.
- A dead end still closes and lands: a cycle abandoned after its opening keeps what is worth
  keeping, reverts the rest, and records what was tried, why it stopped, and what replaces it. Its
  closing is `cycle --close --dead-end`, titled with the cycle title plus " dead-end closing".
''')

    under `#### Rungs` and rewritten into every cycle commit, each marker computed from the cycle's
    commits. It is kept by the closing so the landmark holds it and replaced by the next opening

# ---- Opening
section("### Opening\n","Rungs are named, not numbered",'''### Opening

The cycle's first commit carries its plan: the record `cycle --open` scaffolds is deliberated and
laddered before it is committed, so the opening's review is of the plan, where a wrong direction
costs the least. The user is free to commit the setup first. A single-step cycle does all of it in
its one commit ([Cycle shape](#cycle-shape)). Before that commit
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#opening)):

1. Sync: sync both repos ([Sync](#sync)), whatever the cycle's form.
2. Open: `vc-x1 cycle --open --title "<bare cycle title>"` makes the bookmark on the work `@`,
   kept local, first, so every edit of the cycle is on its branch. It then writes the record: what
   `## Closed` holds is deleted, the `## Todo` entry of that title is moved into the `## In
   Progress` scaffold ([The In Progress block](agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block), the
   specimen in [cycle-model.md](agent-data/cycle-model.md)), and `zTOC.md`'s ladder is replaced
   with the opening and the closing.
3. Waiting: check each `## Waiting` entry's condition, and promote what is met into `## Todo` at
   the rank it names.
4. Deliberate and plan: write the problem, the solution, the acceptance check, and the
   deliberation, and ladder the work rungs, each a `##### ` heading under `#### Rungs` with its
   intent. `vc-x1 cycle --ladder` makes the ladder from the headings. A small cycle's deliberation
   reads `_None._`, and the plan stays provisional, later rungs revising it.
5. Bump: bump the version-of-record to the opening's version ([Suffix
   scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)), by the project's own tool, and the agent-files
   version with it when the cycle is an `agent-files` proposal ([Agent-files
   version](agent-data/versioning.md#agent-files-version)).

''')
# ---- per-rung flow
section("### The per-rung flow\n","### Committing vs pushing\n",'''### The per-rung flow

Every commit (opening, each rung between, closing) goes through these steps, read from here
immediately before acting ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#the-per-rung-flow)). `vc-x1 cycle
--status` says where the cycle stands and which rung is next:

0. Sync: sync both repos ([Sync](#sync)), required at the opening and the closing, optional
   between, the agent's or the user's call.
1. Bump: bump the version-of-record to this commit's version ([Suffix
   scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)), by the project's own tool, the agent-files
   version beside it in an `agent-files` proposal cycle. The version is the project's and `vc-x1`
   never writes it. With `[version]` in the config it refuses a commit that leaves the version
   unchanged, and `--same-version`, which commits anyway, is the user's to allow.
2. Work: do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop ([Stop and
   ask](#stop-and-ask)).
3. Rung subsection: write what this rung changed, conceptually, into its subsection under `####
   Rungs`.
4. Validate: `vc-x1 validate` before every review, doc-only commits included. The full run rewrites
   files (`cargo fmt`), so use `--fast` while a review iterates. A failure is read and its cause
   named before validation runs again, and a failure that does not repeat is a finding, reported
   and given a Todo entry. A rung that changes the artifact then installs the working copy's dev
   build, `vc-x1 install --profile dev`, so the review runs the code under review, and again after
   each review fix ([Dev artifact name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)). A rung has
   its own test and no more, the acceptance check being the closing's.
5. Work review: stop before writing any description and say "please review", as its own message
   with no title or body. The review is of the working-copy diff ([jj
   basics](agent-data/jj.md#jj-basics)). Iterate over steps 2 through 5 until the user approves
   with "continue" or "go".
6. Describe: write the description in [Commit-body form](agent-data/prose.md#commit-body-form),
   read from the file first with its specimen, [commit-model.md](agent-data/commit-model.md)
   ([Commit description](#commit-description)). A local description can still be changed before
   the Land, so it has no review of its own.
7. Commit: after approval, the work and agent repos are committed locally by `vc-x1 cycle --commit
   --title "..." --body "..."`, a pair ([Committing vs pushing](#committing-vs-pushing)). The
   cycle's first commit is its opening and needs neither. The ladder is rewritten into the commit,
   the rung `(done)` and the next `(current)`, so no marker is typed or flipped. The closing is
   `vc-x1 cycle --close` ([Cycle shape](#cycle-shape), [Close-out](#close-out)). A rung that
   changes the artifact then installs its dev build again, so the next rung runs the committed
   code, not the working copy's ([Dev artifact name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)).
''')
# ---- Committing vs pushing
section("### Committing vs pushing\n","#### A cycle is local by default\n",'''### Committing vs pushing

A cycle's commits are made *by* `vc-x1 cycle`, a rung by `--commit` and the closing by `--close`,
never by `jj commit`, and published only by a push
([why](agent-data/rationale.md#committing-vs-pushing)).

- `cycle --commit`, `--close`, and `--land` stay on this machine and need no approval.
- `--push` on any of them publishes, exactly like `vc-x1 push`, as does `squash-push`. With
  `--commit` or `--close` it is a draft push, of the cycle's bookmark, and with `--land` it is the
  publish, of the target.
- `vc-x1 squash` continues a rung, folding the working copy into it. `squash --title --body` is the
  sanctioned re-describe of `@-`. `vc-x1 commit` is the plain commit of a pair, for work outside a
  cycle, and `commit -r REV --title --body` describes a commit made by hand.
- A bare `jj commit` is asked for by name and is for local saves and [local ladder](#local-ladders)
  intermediates, which collapse before the rung commits. What the commands do is in [vc-x1 commit
  and push][vpush].
''')
sub('''- The default: every commit is `vc-x1 commit -s b`, a pair, the agent commit holding the session
  to that moment, and the opening's bookmark created and not pushed.
- Any mix of work and agent commits is valid. `commit -s b` makes a 1:1 pair, `commit -s w` rungs
  then `commit -s a --covers <REVSET>` or the Land make N:1,''','''- The default: every commit is `vc-x1 cycle --commit`, a pair, the agent commit holding the session
  to that moment, and the opening's bookmark created and not pushed.
- Any mix of work and agent commits is valid. `cycle --commit` makes a 1:1 pair, `cycle --commit -s
  w` rungs then `commit -s a --covers <REVSET>` or the Land make N:1,''')
sub('''- A backup, a move between machines, or someone else to see the cycle publishes mid-cycle by
  `push -s b`,''','''- A backup, a move between machines, or someone else to see the cycle publishes mid-cycle by a
  draft push, `push -s b`,''')
# ---- Pushing
sub('''Pushing is by `vc-x1 push`, and the Land's bookmark moves are `vc-x1 land` and `delete-bookmark`.''','''Pushing is by `vc-x1 push` or a stage's `--push`, and the Land's bookmark moves are `cycle --land`'s
and `delete-bookmark`'s.''')
sub('''  `squash-push` and refused by `land` and `commit`, and the `--yes` flag answers, so the agent
  passes it only for a forced push the user approved.''','''  `squash-push` and refused by `cycle` and `commit`, and the `--yes` flag answers, so the agent
  passes it only for a forced push the user approved.''')
sub('''delegated cycles follows each `land --push` with the next cycle's opening,''','''delegated cycles follows each `cycle --land --push` with the next cycle's opening,''')
# ---- Close-out
section("### Close-out\n","### Local ladders\n",'''### Close-out

The cycle's last commit is bookkeeping and its body describes that bookkeeping. A single-step cycle
does all of it in its one commit, step 5 aside ([Cycle shape](#cycle-shape)):

1. Acceptance check: run the check the opening stated, as the first thing in closing, and record
   pass or fail. A rung may run it and the closing record the result, since some checks run only
   mid-ladder. A failure is a finding, and why it failed is determined.
2. Finalize the cycle-record in place ([Cycle-record](#cycle-record)):
   - sync the title if the scope shifted, and every anchor back-reference with it. A published rung
     title and the bookend pair keep their names, so a rename then reaches the block's text and the
     rungs not yet published only
   - replace the provisional solution statement with what was done
   - add the design subsections the deliberation grew
   - complete the closing rung's subsection
   - ask what in the block must outlive the cycle, and write it into the `notes/` file it
     belongs to
   - the block is moved whole to `## Closed`, leaving `## In Progress` reading
     `_No cycle currently in progress._`, and `zTOC.md`'s ladder is rewritten with every marker
     final, both by `vc-x1 cycle --close`.
3. Validate: full validation, and update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
4. Size: when an agent-file changed, record the line count in `notes/agent-files-size.md`,
   smaller being the quasi-goal. A cycle that touched none adds no row.
5. Close-out shape ([Close-out shapes](agent-data/jj.md#close-out-shapes)): a ladder closes as a
   trapezoid, `cycle --close --trapezoid <target>`, the closing commit carrying the shape, so
   nothing is reshaped at Land.
6. Continuation notes: anything the next agent needs is written into `TODO.md > ## Continuation
   notes`, the first section, before the closing commit, which carries them, so the work-repo is
   clean from the Land on. A fact known only after the Land is not written: the note names what the
   next session checks, `main` at the closing, the bookmarks gone, the installed version's commit.
   The next acquaint reads it first, files or keeps each item, and resets the section ([Todo
   format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format)).
7. Test the closed cycle: the acceptance check again, as the last thing, on the closed tree. It is
   the first run on that tree when a merge brought the target's changes in, and otherwise a
   confirmation the user may skip. A fault found here stops the flow ([Stop and
   ask](#stop-and-ask)), and the way back is the user's choice: reopen the cycle, fix inside the
   closing, fix on top, or their own, the test itself being what may be wrong.
8. Land: on the user's go, the sequence in [Land](agent-data/jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land).
   A Land is a fast-forward, and a target that moved is refused naming the ways on: a merge at the
   Land, `cycle --land <target> --merge`, which the user asks for and which lands a tree no rung
   validated, the closing made again, or a rebase.
9. Restart: the user restarts the agent.
''')

content.text:
**On the rung's position.** I'd append it as rung 12, after the docs rung, rather than insert it as 11. The docs rung is already committed, and the ladder's order is checked against the commits: a new rung placed above a done one shows as "done below current" until it commits, and the history would then disagree with the ladder for good. Reordering the commits instead means a `jj rebase` through `TODO.md`, `zTOC.md`, and the version line in every rung, which is the own-conflict problem we filed. Appending costs nothing: the rung updates the command lines in the agent-files itself, and the set goes to `v0.3.1-10`.

**On the agent-repo's `main`.** I can read "moving it too" two ways, and they differ a lot, so tell me which you mean.

- **Reading A: advance the agent `main` locally at each cycle commit**, as the work-repo's cycle bookmark advances. Today `cycle --commit` makes the agent commit but leaves `main` behind it, and only a push or a Land sets it.
  - This keeps the agent-repo linear, so it bends no rule. It only changes when the bookmark moves.
  - It would make the two repos read the same after a commit: each has a bookmark on its latest commit, and `cycle --status` could report the agent side the same way.
  - The cost is the at-rest invariant. `validate-agent` assumes `main` equals `main@origin` except inside a push, so mid-cycle it would report a mismatch that is now normal. That check, and the wording in At rest, would need to mean "unpublished" rather than "lost".
  - `push`, the Land, and `squash-push` each set `main` themselves, so they would become no-ops on that step, not conflicts.

- **Reading B: give the agent-repo its own bookmark per cycle**, mirroring the work-repo's.
  - This is the one the rules warn against: `jj.md` says a mirrored agent bookmark steers session pushes at the wrong remote ref.
  - The journal is one stream per session, not per cycle, so a branch per cycle only fits if sessions and cycles line up one to one.
  - It is also what the Todo entry **vc-x2: the agent-repo stays on main, agent branches set aside** already defers.

**On orthogonal.** Reading A is orthogonal to the `-s` rung: it touches the commit's agent half and `validate-agent`, not the parser. I'd make it its own rung, marked as an experiment in the record, so it can be backed out alone. Reading B is not orthogonal to much of anything; it reaches into push, Land, sync, and the session symlink, and I'd keep it out of this cycle.

My lean is A as a rung after the `-s` one, if that is the reading you meant.

Understood on both, and that changes my answer.

**Work-repo: insert as rung 11.** The branch is local past the opening, so rewriting it is allowed and the links survive it, since every `ochid:` is a change id and a rebase keeps those. The plan would be:

- `jj new --insert-after` the removal rung, so the docs commit rebases onto the new one automatically.
- Do the `-s` work there, with its rung heading placed before the docs rung's heading in `TODO.md`.
- Rework the docs commit after: it will conflict in the version line, `Cargo.lock`, `zTOC.md`, and `TODO.md`, and its command lines gain `-s b`. It becomes `0.85.22-12`, and its tree is validated again.
- Regenerate the ladder in both commits, so docs reads 12 and the closing 13.

One snag: `cycle --commit` cannot commit an inserted rung. It commits `@` and advances the cycle's bookmark, which must be at or below the commit, and here the bookmark sits above it on the docs commit. The way that works today is to make the commit with `jj`, then stamp it with `vc-x1-dev commit -s b -r <rev> --no-advance`, which describes a draft in place. That is a gap in the tool worth noting in the rung: an inserted rung is exactly the "unplanned work" case the protocol describes.

**Agent-repo: inserting a node.** I had the wrong reading; you mean putting the new rung's agent commit at the matching position in the agent line, with `main` untouched since it is still at `origin`'s. Thoughts:

- It is mechanically the same move, `jj rebase -r <agent commit> --insert-after <rung 10's agent commit>`, and nothing published is rewritten.
- The difference is the content. A work commit's diff is independent edits; an agent commit's diff is lines appended to the session transcript. Moving an append earlier puts it against a file that does not yet hold the lines before it, so I expect conflicts in the `.jsonl` in the moved commit and again in the docs agent commit rebased over it.
- Those conflicts resolve to the same final tree, but the intermediate trees would then hold transcript lines out of the order they happened. The graph would be symmetric and the journal's chronology at those two commits would be false.
- The pairing does not need it: the trailers link by change id, so an agent commit at the tip pairs with a work commit in the middle just as well.

So as an experiment it is cheap and reversible with `jj undo`, and I think the thing it tests is whether an append-only journal can be reordered without conflicts. My guess is no, and that the finding will be "the work-repo reorders, the agent-repo pairs by id and stays in time order". But that is worth knowing from a try, not from my guess.

**Suggested order:** the work-repo insert and the docs rework first, validated; then the agent-repo insert as its own step, with the op id noted beforehand so it backs out alone. Say go and I'll start, or tell me if you want the agent-repo try done first.

That makes sense, and it reverses my order: the agent-repo node goes in first, so the session's record of the work accrues in it while the work is done, instead of being made at the tip and moved after.

**How it would go.**

- In the agent-repo, `jj new --insert-after <rung 10's agent commit> --insert-before <docs' agent commit>`. That makes the new node the agent `@`, with the docs agent commit and the current uncommitted tail rebased above it. `main` is untouched.
- Then the work-repo insert, the `-s` work, and the commit of the pair, the work half stamped by `commit -r`, as before.
- After the commit, `jj commit` on a mid-line `@` leaves the new empty `@` beside the docs commit, not above it, so the agent `@` is put back on the tip by hand.

**What worries me: the agent `@` is the live session.**

- Moving `@` checks out an older tree. The transcript file on disk would be rewritten to what it held at rung 10, while the harness is still appending to it. The later lines are safe in the commits above, but I cannot say what the harness does when the file changes under it: it may keep writing, or write to a file that is no longer the one on disk.
- This session is one transcript file, and both the docs agent commit and the new node would append to it from the same point. So the docs commit conflicts the moment the new node gains a line, and every snapshot after re-conflicts it.
- Resolved either way, the file at the new node holds lines written after the docs lines, placed before them.

**What I think makes it clean: a session boundary.**

- Each session writes its own transcript file. If the node is inserted and then you restart me, the new session's file is new, so the inserted node adds a file and touches nothing the docs commit touched. No conflict, and no live file is rewritten under a running session.
- The node then holds exactly the session that did the `-s` work, which is the thing you want captured, and its position in the line matches the work commit's.
- The tail of this session, this discussion included, stays as the commit above the docs agent commit, to be folded into it or kept as its own.

**So my suggestion** is to make the insert the last act of this session: note the op ids, insert the agent node, write a continuation note saying where both repos stand and how to back out, and stop for your restart. The next session acquaints, finds its `@` mid-line by design, and does the rung.

**What the experiment would tell us**, whichever way it goes: whether the agent-repo can take a rung inserted mid-line at all, and whether "one session per rung" is the condition that makes it work. If it is, that is a rule worth having for vc-x2. The parts I have not verified are how the harness behaves when `@` moves under it, and whether `cycle --commit` and the Land cope with an agent `@` that is not the head; the Land reads the agent `@-` in places, so I'd expect at least one refusal to work through.

Agreed, and appending is the lower-risk choice: nothing committed is rewritten, the tool commits the rung as it is built to, and both repos stay in time order.

**The appended rung.**

- It becomes rung 12, its heading placed before the closing's in `TODO.md`, and `cycle --ladder` renumbers the closing to 13.
- A title that fits the 50-character limit: `feat: cycle requires -s on commit, close, land`.
- `-s` is required with `--commit`, `--close`, and `--land`, and still refused with `--open`, `--ladder`, and `--status`. With `--land` it takes `b` or `p`, and in a chain one `-s` serves both stages.
- What follows it: the tests and the rehearsal script gain `-s b`, the README's examples and its scope table change, and the workspace-detecting default goes.
- The agent-files' command lines gain `-s b` too. The docs rung is already committed, so this rung edits them and the set moves to `v0.3.1-10`. The version is `0.85.22-12`, by `cargo xtask bump next`.

**The Todo entry.**

- Your title as written, `feat: add a capability in vc-x1 to insert rung with -sw|a|b|p`, is 61 characters. That is fine for a Todo entry, but it would be over the limit as a cycle title, so it gets shortened when the cycle opens, or I shorten it now if you prefer.
- I'd file it in `## Todo` in this rung's commit, since the rung is what raised it, and have it carry what we worked out, so the experiment starts from it:
  - The work-repo takes an inserted rung by `jj new --insert-after`, and the commits above conflict in the version line, `Cargo.lock`, `zTOC.md`, and `TODO.md`.
  - `cycle --commit` cannot commit one today, since the cycle's bookmark is above the commit, so the pair is stamped by `commit -r`.
  - The agent-repo's node has to go in first, so the session's record of the work accrues in it.
  - The open risks: the agent `@` is the live session and moving it rewrites the transcript file on disk, the same transcript appended from two commits conflicts, and one session per rung may be what makes it clean.
  - The Land reads the agent `@-` in places and has not been tried with an agent `@` that is not the head.
- It relates to **Two cycles in flight conflict in the record and the version**, which is the same conflict seen from another side, so the two entries should cite each other.

**One question the entry raises:** what the scope flag means for an insert. `-s w` and `-s p` are clear. `-s a` alone, an agent node with no work rung, I can't picture a use for yet, so I'd record it as part of the experiment to decide, not as a requirement.

Say go and I'll do the rung, appended, with the Todo entry in it.

**`-s a` as a side conversation.** That reading fits what the tool already has, so it needs little that is new:

- Off topic, no `ochid:`: this is today's `commit -s a`, an unpaired agent commit with no trailer.
- Related to an earlier rung: this is `commit -s a --covers <REV>`, whose `ochid:` names the work commit. The rules already allow several agent commits naming one work commit.
- So for the agent side the new part is only the position. And since the link is by change id, a side conversation appended at the tip is already tied to its rung. Inserting it buys adjacency in the graph, at the cost of the transcript conflicts we talked through. I'd record `-s a` in the Todo as "append with `--covers` may be all it needs, the experiment decides".

**Is insert dangerous?** I agree it is not, in the sense that matters:

- While the commits above are local, an insert only rebases them, and `jj undo` takes it back. Nothing is lost.
- What makes it risky is the same thing that makes `squash` risky: commits above that are published. The tool already has that line drawn. `squash` warns on a published draft and refuses one in jj's `immutable()` without `--ignore-immutable`, and the push that follows a rewrite is a forced push, which has its own approval.
- So I'd have insert follow `squash` exactly, and add no `--yes`. We decided two rungs ago that `--yes` means "the user approved a forced push" and should not become a switch for any question, which is why the version check got `--same-version`. Requiring `--yes` here would undo that.

**Delete or remove is the dangerous one**, and I'd file it as its own Todo. Thoughts on it:

- It discards work, where insert only moves it. jj's operation log still holds it, but nobody should have to know that to be safe.
- The codebase has a precedent that fits better than `--yes`: `fix-desc` and `fix-todo` are dry-run by default and write only with `--no-dry-run`. A remove that shows what it would drop, and drops it only when told, makes the look come first.
- The agent side is the hard part. Removing a work rung leaves its agent commit's `ochid:` naming nothing. The journal should never be deleted, so the agent commit stays, and the question is what its trailer says after. `trailers` already knows a `lost` state, which may be the answer.
- The record follows: the rung's heading goes, and the ladder is made again.

**How they relate.** Insert, remove, and reorder are one family, reshaping a ladder while it is local. I'd still keep two entries, since they differ in risk: the insert experiment as you titled it, and a second for remove, each citing the other. Reorder can be a line in the first.

content.text:
Yes, in two ways, and there is a third option that avoids the question.

**1. Cargo's `split-debuginfo`.**

```toml
[profile.release]
debug = true
split-debuginfo = "packed"
```

On Linux this writes the DWARF to a `vc-x1.dwp` file beside the binary, and the binary keeps only small skeleton references. `"unpacked"` leaves it as `.dwo` files in `target/` instead. The catch is the reader: `gdb` handles split DWARF well, but `perf`'s support for `.dwp` has been patchy, and I have not tested it with the perf 7.3 on this machine. It may resolve function names and still miss inlined frames and line numbers.

**2. A classic separate debug file.** Build with `debug = true`, then split it after the build:

```
objcopy --only-keep-debug target/release/vc-x1 vc-x1.debug
strip --strip-debug target/release/vc-x1
objcopy --add-gnu-debuglink=vc-x1.debug target/release/vc-x1
```

The binary ends up the size it is today plus a few bytes for the link. `perf` and `gdb` both find the `.debug` file by that link or by build id, and this is the form distributions ship, so tool support is solid. Cargo has no setting that does it, so it would be two more lines in `[build] commands` or an xtask.

**3. A separate profile, which I'd recommend.** Leave `release` untouched and add one that inherits from it:

```toml
[profile.profiling]
inherits = "release"
debug = "line-tables-only"
```

Then the shipped binary does not change at all, and a `[profile.profiling]` table in `.vc-config.md` makes it `vc-x1 build --profile profiling`, which fits how `dev` and `release` are already set up. `line-tables-only` gives perf function names, inlined frames, and line numbers at a fraction of full debug info's size, and where the info lives stops mattering because that binary is never installed.

Two notes on what it would have changed today:

- The function names in my profile came from the symbol table, which the release binary already has. What was missing was the callers, since most of the hot code was inlined. Debug info fixes that.
- Adding `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` to the profiling profile would let `perf record -g --user-callchains` walk the stack cheaply. Today's run used DWARF unwinding and wrote a 50 MB data file for seven seconds.

I have not changed anything. If you want the profiling profile, it is a small addition to `Cargo.toml` and `.vc-config.md`, and it could go in the Todo entry for the lookup work or be done on its own.

Today it does one job, the version, and you run it through a cargo alias from anywhere inside the repo:

```
cargo xtask version              # prints 0.85.22-12
cargo xtask bump next            # 0.85.22-12 -> 0.85.22-13, Cargo.lock refreshed
cargo xtask bump bare            # drops the suffix, a close-out's version
cargo xtask bump 0.86.0-0        # sets it as written
cargo xtask                      # prints the usage line
```

**How it is wired.**

- `.cargo/config.toml` defines the alias: `xtask = "run --quiet --package xtask --"`. Cargo finds that file by walking up from the current directory, so it works from any subdirectory.
- The code is the `xtask/` package, a member of the workspace the root `Cargo.toml` now declares. The first run compiles it, and `--quiet` hides that, so the first call pauses for a few seconds.
- It finds the manifest from its own location at compile time, not from where you run it, so it always edits this repo's `Cargo.toml`.

**How to test it.**

- Its unit tests: `cargo test -p xtask`. They cover the suffix arithmetic and that the manifest's comments and layout survive an edit.
- It is in the workspace's default members, so `vc-x1 validate` already formats, lints, and tests it with everything else.
- By hand, safely: `bump` writes to the real `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock`. Mostly it doesn't. The xtask pattern is a convention, not a cargo feature, and completion for it is a known gap. What people do falls into a few groups:

**1. Go without.** This is the common case. The original cargo-xtask write-up says nothing about completion, and most projects that use the pattern have a handful of task names and just type them.

**2. Give the task runner its own name.** This is how the largest example handles it. The Rust compiler's own repo does not use `cargo xtask`; it has a wrapper called `x` (`./x build`, `./x test`), and it ships generated completion scripts for that name, made with `clap_complete`. Because the command is `x` and not `cargo`, the shell asks the right program and there is nothing to intercept. Projects that use `just` or `cargo-make` (through its `makers` binary) get completion the same way: a standalone name with its own script.

**3. Lean on the shell's cargo completion.** Cargo's shipped scripts complete subcommand and alias names. I believe the zsh one goes a step further and hands off to a completion function for `cargo-<name>` when one is defined, which is how installed plugins such as `cargo-nextest` can complete; I'm less sure the bash script does the same, and I have not checked either on this machine. Either way that route is for an installed `cargo-foo` binary, not for an alias that expands to `cargo run -p xtask`.

**4. Wait for cargo's native completion.** Cargo has been moving its completion onto clap's dynamic engine, the same one `vc-x1` uses, where the shell asks the binary. It has been an unstable, nightly-only feature, and I don't know its current state or whether it will reach through an alias to the program behind it. If it does, this problem goes away upstream.

So the honest summary is: there is no standard answer for `cargo xtask <tab>`, and the projects that care sidestep it with a standalone name.

**For this repo**, that points at option 2 as the cleaner long-term fit than the `.bashrc` wrapper I sketched. A small `x` at the repo root that runs the xtask, with the xtask on clap and registered for completion the way `vc-x1` is, would complete without touching cargo's function. `cargo xtask` would keep working as the conventional spelling. It also lines up with where you are heading: if validate, build, and install move out of `vc-x1`, they need a short name people type many times a day.

Parts of this are from memory, not checked here: the zsh hand-off and the status of cargo's native completion in particular. I can verify both against the installed cargo and its docs before anything is decided on them.

Your reading of that recipe is right, and it is telling what it leaves out. Those three steps make a completion script for the xtask binary under its own name. That works when you run the binary as `xtask <tab>`. It does not make `cargo xtask <tab>` work, because the shell still asks cargo's function for anything that starts with `cargo`. So the recipe is option 2 without saying so.

On what the Rust teams do, as far as I know and without having checked today:

- The compiler team does use completion. They get it by not using `cargo xtask` at all: their runner is `x`, and its completion scripts are generated and checked into the repo.
- Cargo's own repo, I believe, has a few `xtask-*` aliases for maintenance jobs, a handful of names typed rarely. I don't know of any completion for them beyond the alias names, and I can't speak to what individual maintainers have in their shells.
- Whether cargo's native completion will ever reach through an alias is something I'd have to look up, so I would not plan around it.

So "own name" is what people who care actually do, and I agree with where that points you.

On the bigger question, I think yesterday's decision and today's finding fit together better than they first look:

- **The decision stands**: the cycle tool should know nothing about the work. Validate, build, run, and install are the app's.
- **But an xtask is a poor home for them in other repos.** It is Rust-only, it needs a workspace member in every repo, and as you found it has no completion. Your `wt-21-6` case, a repo that is not this one and may not be Rust, is exactly where it falls down.
- **What `vc-x1 validate|build|install` gives is not Rust-specific at all.** It is a runner of command lists named in a config file, with the same commands and working completion in every repo. That is worth keeping; it just does not belong inside the cycle tool.

So the shape I'd suggest for vc-x2 is two names, not one tool and an xtask:

- The cycle tool, which manages the repo and its history.
- A small task runner under its own name, which reads the lists from the config and runs them. Its completion can offer the task names from the config itself, so a repo's own tasks complete without anyone writing a script.

The cycle tool then calls the runner at its gates, or just a configured command, which is the "hook" we wrote into the deliberation. This repo's `cargo xtask bump` stays what it is, one project's own task, and could equally be a line in that config.

content.text:
You were right to doubt it: it is solved, at least for bash and zsh, and I found the mechanism and tested it here.

**Stable cargo forwards unknown subcommands to their own completion.** Since cargo 1.87 (merged March 2025), cargo's bash script does this for any subcommand it has no options for: it rewrites the word to `cargo-<name>` and asks bash-completion to complete that command instead. The zsh script has had the same hook for longer, calling a `_cargo-<name>` function if one is defined. It was added for installed plugins like `cargo asm`, but the script does not check whether the word is a plugin or an alias.

So for `cargo xtask`, all it takes is a completion registered under the name `cargo-xtask`. I tested that with the cargo 1.99 script installed here and bash-completion 2.18:

```
complete -W "version bump" cargo-xtask
cargo xt<tab>        -> xtask
cargo xtask v<tab>   -> version
cargo xtask b<tab>   -> bump
```

No wrapper around cargo's function is needed, which is what I told you earlier and was wrong about. My simulated empty-word case (`cargo xtask <tab>`) returned nothing; I think that is my test harness and not the mechanism, but I have not confirmed it in a live shell.

**What this means for an xtask on clap:** it registers its dynamic completion under the bin name `cargo-xtask`, and `cargo xtask <tab>` then asks the xtask binary itself. That is the same engine `vc-x1` uses, so task names and flags complete without a hard-coded list. It needs bash-completion 2.12 or later, so macOS's default bash falls back to file names.

**The cargo team's own direction** is native completion, where cargo answers for itself through clap:

- It is still nightly-only, enabled with `CARGO_COMPLETE=bash cargo +nightly`, and the tracking issue is open.
- It completes alias names from the config.
- "Completing arguments after an alias" is on its checklist with no linked PR, and delegating to third-party subcommands is listed as a future extension. A user asked in November 2025 how to complete their own subcommand's flags and the page shows no answer.
- A maintainer noted the bash forwarding above would be "short-lived" unless someone carries it into the native work, and another said losing it would not block the switch.

So the stable path works today and the future path has not caught up to it yet.

**One thing specific to your shell:** your `cargo` completion is not cargo's script. It is registered to `_carapace_completer`, so carapace answers for `cargo` and the forwarding above never runs. Whether carapace forwards to a `cargo-xtask` completion, or needs a spec of its own for it, I have not checked.

This weakens my "give it its own name" argument for Rust repos: `cargo xtask` can complete properly. It does not change the point about your other repos, where an xtask is Rust-only and a config-driven runner is not.

Sources:
- [Tracking Issue for native-completion, rust-lang/cargo#14520](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/14520)
- [feat(cli): forward bash completions of third party subcommands, rust-lang/cargo#15247](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/15247)
- [Add custom completer for `cargo <TAB>` to complete aliases, rust-lang/cargo#15319](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/15319)

Yes, that is where it goes: the xtask parses its arguments by hand today, so completion means moving it to clap and adding `clap_complete`, in `xtask/src/main.rs` and `xtask/Cargo.toml`.

Two things in what you pasted:

**That is not really help.** The xtask has no `-h` or `--help`. Both fell into its "anything else" arm, which prints the usage line to stderr and exits with a failure status. It reads like help by accident. Moving to clap fixes this too: you get real `-h` and `--help`, per-task help, and proper exit codes, along with completion.

**Your `cx` alias will not complete on its own.** Bash completes by the first word typed, and it does not expand aliases to find a completion, so `cx <tab>` looks for something registered under `cx` and finds nothing. The good news is that it is the easy case: `cx` takes exactly the words a `cargo-xtask` completion expects, the ones after the command. So whatever gets registered for `cargo-xtask` can be registered for `cx` as well, with no cargo forwarding involved. With the throwaway line from before, that is:

```
complete -W "version bump" cargo-xtask cx
```

and once the xtask is on clap, its completion is registered under both names the same way.

That makes `cx` the short standalone name we talked about, and it sidesteps carapace entirely, since nothing but your own line registers `cx`.

The per-repo wrinkle still applies: `cx` in another repo runs that repo's xtask, so the registration has to ask whichever xtask is in the current directory.

Nothing is changed in the repo. This fits with the Todo entry **Build config moves to an xtask**, since that is when there are enough tasks to make it worth it. I can add the clap move and the completion to that entry, or file it separately. Which would you like?

You can get used to `cx`. What you should not get used to is a fixed word list behind it, like my `complete -W "version bump"` example, because that would offer this repo's tasks in every repo.

The name and the answer are separate things:

- **The name** is what bash looks up, and `cx` is the same in every repo. That part is fine.
- **The answer** has to come from the repo you are standing in, since `cx` there runs that repo's xtask.

So `cx` gets one generic completion function in `.bashrc`, and that function does not know any task names itself. It asks the current repo's xtask, by running it in completion mode, and passes back whatever it says. Then:

- In this repo, `cx <tab>` offers `version` and `bump`, and later `validate`, `build`, and so on.
- In another repo, it offers that repo's tasks.
- In a repo with no xtask, or one whose xtask does not answer completion requests, it offers nothing, and the function has to stay quiet about it.

That works when each xtask follows the same convention, which with clap is the dynamic completion `vc-x1` already uses. So the convention is something each of your apps' xtasks would adopt, and one shared snippet or small crate could carry it so it is not rewritten per app.

The cost is the one I mentioned: each tab press starts cargo to reach the xtask, and rebuilds it first if its source changed. I have not measured it; I'd expect a noticeable fraction of a second when it is built and much longer on the first press after an edit.

That delay, and needing the convention in every repo, is the argument for the other design: one installed runner that reads each repo's tasks from its config file. It completes instantly and needs nothing added to each app. `cx` could point at either, so the habit carries over whichever you choose.
One rung, yes: the xtask moves to clap, gains real `-h`, and answers completion for `cargo xtask` and `cx`. Starting it, appended as rung 13.

No, and that is the one unusual thing about it. The file is the same for every app, because it contains no task names at all. The app-specific part happens later, each time you press tab.

What the function does when you press tab is run this, in whatever directory you are in:

```
COMPLETE=bash cargo xtask -- <the words you typed>
```

That starts the xtask of the repo you are standing in, and that xtask prints the candidates. So:

| Where you are | What `cx <tab>` asks | What comes back |
|---|---|---|

content.text:
Bash's completion has three parts: a function that produces candidates, a registration that says which command names use it, and the call bash makes on each tab.

## 1. `source` defines the function in your shell

`source ~/.config/cargo-xtask-completion.bash` runs the file inside your current shell, not in a child process. So the function `_cargo_xtask_complete` becomes part of the shell, the same way a function written at the prompt would, and the `complete` line at the end runs in the shell too. Without `source`, both would vanish when the file finished running.

## 2. `complete` registers the function for command names

```
complete -o nospace -o bashdefault -F _cargo_xtask_complete cargo-xtask cx
```

This tells bash: when completing a line whose first word is `cargo-xtask` or `cx`, call `_cargo_xtask_complete` to get the candidates. `complete -p cx` shows what is registered for a name. Bash keeps one registration per name, and the last one wins.

The options:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-F _cargo_xtask_complete` | the function to call |
| `-o nospace` | don't add a space after a completed word automatically; the function decides |
| `-o bashdefault` | if the function returns nothing, fall back to bash's own completion, mostly file names |
| `-o nosort` | keep the candidates in the order given, instead of alphabetical |

The line you quoted is the version from before yesterday's change. If you regenerated the file after the `nosort` change, it now ends with an `if` on the bash version: bash 4.4 and later gets the line with `-o nosort`, and older bash gets the line without it, since older bash rejects that option.

## 3. What happens on tab

Say you type `cx bump n` and press tab. Before calling the function, bash sets some variables describing the line:

| Variable | Value here |
|---|---|
| `COMP_WORDS` | the words: `(cx bump n)` |
| `COMP_CWORD` | index of the word being completed: `2` |
| `COMP_LINE` / `COMP_POINT` | the whole line, and the cursor's position in it |
| `COMP_TYPE` | which kind of tab: first press, second press to list, and so on |

It calls the function with three arguments: `$1` is the command (`cx`), `$2` is the word being completed (`n`), and `$3` is the word before it (`bump`).

The function's only job is to fill the array `COMPREPLY`. When it returns, bash takes what is in `COMPREPLY`. One candidate gets inserted into the line, and several get listed on screen.

## 4. What our function does

It does not know any task names. It asks the program:

```bash
local IFS=$'\013'
...
COMPREPLY=( $( \
    _CLAP_IFS="$IFS" \
    _CLAP_COMPLETE_INDEX="$_CLAP_COMPLETE_INDEX" \
    ...
    COMPLETE="bash" \
    cargo xtask -- "${words[@]}" 2> /dev/null \
) )
```

Step by step:

1. **The words are copied, with one fix.** `words` is a copy of `COMP_WORDS`. Bash splits words at characters like `=` and `:`, so `COMP_WORDS` can disagree with what you think of as the word. Setting `words[COMP_CWORD]="$2"` puts bash's own current word back in.
2. **It runs `cargo xtask` with `COMPLETE=bash` in its environment.** The `_CLAP_COMPLETE_INDEX` variable says which word is being completed. The words follow `--`, so cargo passes them through to the xtask untouched.
3. **The xtask answers instead of running.** The first line of its `main` is `CompleteEnv::with_factory(Cli::command).complete()`. When `COMPLETE` is set, that clap call parses the words, works out what can come next (`next` here), prints the candidates, and exits. The task code never runs.
4. **The output is split into the array.** clap separates candidates with a vertical tab (`\013`) rather than a newline or space, so a candidate containing a space survives. `IFS=$'\013'` makes `$( )` split on that same character, and the parentheses around it turn the pieces into `COMPREPLY`.
5. **Failure falls back to file names.** If `cargo xtask` exits with an error, for example when you are not in a repo, the function clears `COMPREPLY`. With nothing in it, `-o bashdefault` makes bash complete file names instead. That is why you saw file names before the file was sourced.
6. **The space after a word is decided per candidate.** Since `-o nospace` turned off the automatic space, the function re-enables it (`compopt +o nospace`). It turns it off again only when the candidate ends in `=`, `/` or `:`, where you are meant to keep typing.

`2> /dev/null` stops cargo's build messages from printing over your prompt.

## 5. How `cargo xtask <tab>` reaches the same function

Nothing registers our function for `cargo`; cargo's own script is registered for that, as `_cargo`. When you type `cargo xtask bump <tab>`:

1. Bash calls `_cargo`, because the first word is `cargo`.
2. `_cargo` sees a subcommand it has no options for, `xtask`. It replaces that word with `cargo-xtask` and calls bash-completion's `_comp_command_offset`.
3. That function completes the rest of the line as if it began with `cargo-xtask bump`. It drops the leading `cargo` and looks up the registration for `cargo-xtask`.
4. That registration is our function. It runs with words `(cargo-xtask bump "")`, and clap ignores the first word.

So `cx` reaches the function directly, by its own registration, and `cargo xtask` reaches it through cargo's hand-off. Both only work in a shell where the file has been sourced, which is why the `source` line belongs in `.bashrc`.

**The plain version:** `source` loads a function into your shell, and `complete` tells bash "for `cx` and `cargo-xtask`, ask this function". On each tab bash calls it with the typed words, and whatever it puts in `COMPREPLY` becomes the suggestions. Our function holds no task names: it runs `cargo xtask` in a special mode where the xtask prints its possible next words instead of doing anything, so the suggestions always come from whichever repo you are in.

A few, mostly about Rust in a repo that started without it:

- **Make sure `target/` is ignored before the first build.** jj snapshots every file in the working copy, so a build directory that isn't ignored lands in the next commit, megabytes of it. Check the `.gitignore` `vc-x1 init` wrote and add `/target` if it is not there. `cargo init` adds it only when it creates the `.gitignore` itself.
- **Use `cargo init --vcs none`.** The repo is already jj and git, and this stops cargo from deciding anything about version control. Commit `Cargo.lock` too, since it is a binary.
- **The xtask isn't there yet.** `cargo xtask` and `cx` belong to `vc-x1`'s repo. In `wt-21-6`, `cx <tab>` falls back to file names, quietly, which is itself a test of the fallback. To bring the xtask over you need three things:
  - copy `xtask/`
  - copy `.cargo/config.toml`
  - add `[workspace] members = [".", "xtask"]` to the root `Cargo.toml`

  It finds the manifest relative to itself, so it needs no changes.
- **Leave `[version]` out of the config for this first cycle.** Bumping by the xtask needs the xtask, and adding it is itself work. Two ways around that:
  - bump `Cargo.toml` by hand in this cycle and turn the check on later
  - make "add the xtask" the first rung of the cycle, and turn `[version]` on after it

  The first keeps your hello-world cycle about hello world.
- **There is no `[validate]` there either,** so `vc-x1 validate` will refuse with "no `[validate] full` table". That is fine, just expected. `cargo test` and `cargo run -- 5` are your rung tests.
- **The escape hatch.** Refusals are made before anything changes, but if something gets into a state you don't like, `jj op log` and `jj undo` take back the last operation, in either repo.
- **The dev build is one rung behind.** `vc-x1-dev` was last installed at `-12`. Rung 13 changed only the xtask and docs, so behaviour is the same, but `vc-x1 install --profile dev` makes `-V` read `-13`.
- **Findings.** `wt-21-6` has no `TODO.md` of its own until the skeleton goes in. Tell me what you find as you go, and I'll file it in this cycle's record, so the closing carries it.

Thanks for the note on the errors; the refusals naming the next step was the part I cared most about.

You're right. The message is correct only when `main` is behind its `origin`. Here it is ahead: the local "Creating xyz closing" commit was never pushed. So the fix is a push, and a sync would change nothing. The check knows which case it is in, since it has both commit ids, so the message can name the right command:

| Local `main` vs `origin` | What the message should say |
|---|---|
| behind | `vc-x1 sync -s b` brings it up to date |
| ahead | `vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark main` publishes it first |
| diverged | both have moved, and a sync is refused until it is resolved |

The same output shows a second, smaller finding: `land: --source is 'single-step-2', the one local bookmark besides 'main'`. That line comes from `vc-x1 land`'s code and names `--source`, a flag `cycle --land` doesn't have. It should be labelled `cycle --land` and point at `--bookmark`.

- The `+1` in your prompt is only the empty `@` on top of `single-step-2`. Both repos are clean.
- `vc-x1-dev` is still `-12`, as noted. It is safe to keep testing with it.

```
cycle --land: the cycle's bookmark is 'single-step-2', the one local bookmark besides 'main'
error: cycle --land: 'main' is at 467e1c326eac locally and 237129a8cb61 on origin, ahead with commits not yet published: `vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark main` publishes it first
```

What changed, as rung 14, `fix: cycle --land names push for a main ahead`:

- **The refusal reads how local and `origin` stand.**
  - Ahead or absent on `origin`: it names `vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark <target>`, or `-s p` in a plain repo.
  - Behind: it names `vc-x1 sync`.
  - Diverged: it says to reconcile them first and names no command.
  - One function serves both `cycle --land`'s own check and the Land's plan, which had the same wrong wording.
- **The Land's messages are labelled `cycle --land` and name `--bookmark`.** They had said `land:` and `--source`, left from the retired command. With several other bookmarks, it now asks for `--bookmark <NAME>`.
- **Tests:**
  - A new test walks a target through ahead, behind, and diverged and checks each message.
  - A second new test checks the several-bookmarks refusal names `--bookmark` and not `--source`.
  - An existing test in `land.rs` had expected the old "sync first" for an ahead `main`; it now expects the push.
- **Checks:** full validation passes, the rehearsal passes its 48 checks, and `vc-x1-dev` is reinstalled at `-14`.

It is in the working copy, not committed. Step 1 of your plan is the command the message now names.

content.text:
The command to use is:

```
vc-x1-dev push -s b -r main
```

Its dry run on `wt-21-6` says: `publish 'main' where it is, 467e1c326eac, a commit already made`. That is the unpublished xyz closing.

Why `--bookmark main` failed: `push` without `-r` publishes the work `@-`, and in `wt-21-6` that is `single-step-2`'s commit, not `main`'s. `--bookmark` only says which bookmark to set at `@-`. Naming `main` there would have moved `main` forward to `single-step-2`, so `push` refused. Its error does name `-r main` at the end, but "Name one of them" reads as if you hadn't named any.

**The bad advice was mine.** Rung 14's message tells you to run `vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark main`, which is right only when the target sits at `@-`. `-r <target>` publishes the target wherever it is, so it is right in both cases. So that rung's fix is half wrong, and the `-s b` in it is a second small inaccuracy: with `-r`, push sends the work bookmark alone, without the agent half.

That leaves the agent side open: the xyz closing's agent commits are still unpublished. The Land in step 2 commits and publishes the agent `main`, so they go out then.

Two things to fix:

1. **The Land's refusal** should name `vc-x1 push -s b -r <target>`, with a test that runs the named command in an ahead workspace whose `@-` is elsewhere, so the advice is checked and not just matched.
2. **`push`'s own error.** When the bookmark you named isn't the line's, it should say that first and lead with `-r <name>`. "Name one of them" should go.

Rung 14 is already pushed as a draft. These can go in as rung 15, `fix: cycle --land and push name -r for a target`, or I can file them and you carry on with step 1. Which would you like?

What changed:

- **The Land's refusal** names `vc-x1 push -s b -r <target>`. That publishes the target where it is, so it is right whether or not the target sits at `@-`.

- **The test now runs the advice.** It runs the push command the refusal names, in a workspace whose `@-` is not the target, then checks the target is where `origin` is. Rung 14's test only matched the wording, which is how the bad advice got through.
- **An existing `push` test** asserted the old wording; it now checks for the new one.

Two caveats:

- **The messages say `vc-x1`, not `vc-x1-dev`.** That's right once this lands, but while testing you substitute it yourself.
- **`-r` publishes the work bookmark alone.** The xyz closing's agent commits stay unpublished until step 2's Land publishes the agent `main`.

Step 1 worked: `main` and `main@origin` are now the same commit. The xyz closing and its two rungs show `◆`, jj's mark for immutable commits, now that they are published.

Next is step 2, the Land of `single-step-2`:

```
vc-x1-dev cycle --land main -s b --dry-run
vc-x1-dev cycle --land main -s b --push
```

What to expect:

- **A linear fast-forward.** `main` moves to "Create def.txt", taking "Create abc.txt" with it.
- **The bookmark is deleted.** `single-step-2` goes locally, and on `origin` too, since `--push` is given and the branch was pushed.
- **The agent `main` is published.** That includes the xyz commits' agent halves still waiting from step 1.
- **There is no closing commit.** The branch was never closed, and with no `TODO.md` there is no record to say so. That makes this a Land of an unclosed branch, the case we noted.

Rung 15 is still uncommitted in `vc-x1`, waiting for your go after the review. Your run of step 1 used it and worked; that's a good sign but not the review itself.

message.content: In 2. why not dry run the push too: `vc-x1-dev cycle --land main -s b --push --dry-run`?

content.text:
Yes, that's the better check. A dry run should be of the exact command you are about to run, and without `--push` it skips the publish steps:

- pushing `main`
- publishing the agent `main`
- deleting `single-step-2` on `origin`

With `--push --dry-run` it says each of those too, so step 2 becomes:

```
vc-x1-dev cycle --land main -s b --push --dry-run
vc-x1-dev cycle --land main -s b --push
```

One limit to know: the dry run makes every local check and says each step, but it doesn't ask the remote anything. A push that the remote refuses still shows up only on the real run.

content.text:
Your dry run reads right. The one line that misleads is `commit: kept local, `vc-x1 push` publishes it`: in this chain the Land publishes it two lines later. It's the commit code speaking without knowing a Land follows, so it's one more for the findings.

On a required `--single-step` or `--multi-step`, I think you're right, and for a stronger reason than avoiding a guess. The count is unambiguous at no commits and at two or more. At exactly one commit it has to guess, and the guess can do damage:

- **One commit can mean two different things.** It is either a single-step cycle whose opening was committed early, or a ladder where only the opening is done so far, a plan abandoned or rescoped before any work rung.
- **Today the tool always picks the first.** It squashes the closing into the opening and drops the title's " opening". For someone who meant a ladder, that rewrites their opening commit, changes its title, and leaves no closing commit. The dry run says "a single-step cycle", but only if you read it.

So the flag would be a declaration the tool checks against the count, and at one commit it would also choose:

| Commits on the branch | `--single-step` | `--multi-step` |
|---|---|---|
| none | commit `@` as the one commit | refused: there is no opening |
| one | squash into the opening | make a closing commit above it |
| two or more | refused: a ladder can't be squashed | make the closing commit |

That table also covers `--dead-end`, which today is the only way to get a closing commit above a single opening; under the flag it becomes a dead-end title on either shape.

The costs:

- **It reverses a decision.** On the 11th the rationale for the count was that "nothing has to be decided before its first commit". The flag doesn't contradict that: you still decide nothing until the closing, when you know. But the rationale and the Cycle shape section would need rewording to say the count checks the declaration rather than replacing it.
- **One more required flag.** It's the same trade we made for `-s`: explicit beats inferred on a command that writes, and the dry run already shows the inference, so the flag only adds a word.

On naming, I'd use the words the rules already use: "single-step" and "multi-step" are both in Terminology, and `--multi-step` reads better than `--ladder`, which is already a stage flag.

I'd keep it out of this test step. Your dry run shows the inference is right here. It would be a rung of its own, with the findings gathered so far, before the closing.

- **The scaffold's rung subsections** are the defect we expected, now confirmed: a single-step cycle's `## Closed` keeps an opening and a closing subsection for commits that never existed. The opening's text also says "bump the version-of-record", boilerplate that assumes a version this repo doesn't have. So the scaffold's wording carries the agent-files' assumptions into a repo that hasn't adopted them.

# Cycle model

A cycle's `## In Progress` block, shown as a specimen rather than a skeleton: the `config loader`
cycle, mid-run, with its opening landed and its first work rung current. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [The In Progress block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).

One thing the specimen cannot show:

- a single-step cycle drops both bookends and all the steps are in the one commit: the ladder is one
  unlinked rung with the bare title, and there are no rung subsections under it ([Cycle
  shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

## In Progress

### refactor: extract config loader

#### Problem

Config parsing lives inside the CLI entry point, so every subcommand that wants a setting reaches
through `main` for it, and a test cannot load a config without building the CLI.

#### Solution

Move config loading into its own module with a single `load` entry point that the CLI and the tests
call alike.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with a new test that loads a config from a fixture file without touching `main`,
and `vc-x1 config --validate` reports the same findings as before the move.

#### Deliberation

- one work rung, not two: the parser and the loader were going to be split first and moved second,
  but the move is what forces the split, so doing them together is fewer edits
- the acceptance check compares `config --validate` output rather than asserting on internals, so a
  later rename inside the module does not invalidate it

#### Rungs

The rung subsections, in the ladder's order. The ladder itself is in `zTOC.md > ## Ladder`.

##### refactor: extract config loader opening

The cycle's setup commit: create the bookmark, delete `## Closed`'s contents, move the
Todo entry into this block, and bump the version-of-record.

##### refactor: split loader from parser

Loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load without parsing and a test cannot parse
without a file on disk.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config/loader.rs` finds and reads the file, returning the text and its path, so a caller that
    only wants to know which file was read stops here.
  - `config/parser.rs` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands it a string and never
    touches the filesystem.
    - the error type stays shared for now, since splitting it would change the messages
      `config --validate` prints and the acceptance check compares them
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field access moves behind the module
    boundary and the CLI no longer knows the file's shape.

##### refactor: extract config loader closing

Closing out the cycle.


## zTOC.md's ladder

The same cycle's ladder, `zTOC.md > ## Ladder`, its one copy, linking across to the subsections
above:

```
## Ladder

- 0 (done) [refactor: extract config loader opening](TODO.md#refactor-extract-config-loader-opening)
- 1 (current) [refactor: split loader from parser](TODO.md#refactor-split-loader-from-parser)
- [refactor: extract config loader closing](TODO.md#refactor-extract-config-loader-closing)
```

A cycle's record shown as specimens rather than skeletons: the `config loader` cycle, a ladder
mid-run, and the `version flag` cycle, a single-step cycle after its closing. Copy the shape, not
the words. The rules are in [The In Progress block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block) and [Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape).

Who writes what:

- `vc-x1 cycle --open --title` writes the scaffold: the title, the five item headings, the `##
  Todo` entry's text under Problem, the opening and closing rung subsections, and the ladder of
  the two in `zTOC.md`.
- The user and the agent write the rest, the planning being theirs: the items, and each work rung
  as a `#####` heading under `#### Rungs` with its intent, between the bookends.
- The tool makes the ladder from those headings, `cycle --ladder` and every cycle commit, each
  rung's number its position and each marker computed from the commits, so no marker is typed.
- `cycle --close` moves the block to `## Closed`, a single-step cycle's without its `#### Rungs`.

## A ladder, mid-run

The `config loader` cycle with its opening committed and its one work rung current, `TODO.md >
## In Progress`:

```
## In Progress

### refactor: extract config loader

#### Problem

Config parsing lives inside the CLI entry point, so every subcommand that wants a setting reaches
through `main` for it, and a test cannot load a config without building the CLI.

#### Solution

Move config loading into its own module with a single `load` entry point that the CLI and the tests
call alike.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with a new test that loads a config from a fixture file without touching `main`,
and `vc-x1 validate-config` reports the same findings as before the move.

#### Deliberation

- One work rung, not two: the parser and the loader were going to be split first and moved second,
  but the move is what forces the split, so doing them together is fewer edits.
- The acceptance check compares `validate-config`'s output rather than asserting on internals, so a
  later rename inside the module does not invalidate it.

#### Rungs

The rung subsections, in the ladder's order. The ladder itself is in `zTOC.md > ## Ladder`.

##### refactor: extract config loader opening

The cycle's first commit, carrying its plan: the bookmark, the last cycle's record deleted, and the
Todo entry moved into this block.

##### refactor: split loader from parser

Loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load without parsing and a test cannot parse
without a file on disk.

##### refactor: extract config loader closing

Closing out the cycle.
```

The opening and closing subsections are the scaffold's, and the work rung's is the planner's,
written before its commit as an intent of a sentence or two. At the rung's commit the intent gains
its conceptual delta:

```
##### refactor: split loader from parser

Loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load without parsing and a test cannot parse
without a file on disk.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config/loader.rs` finds and reads the file, returning the text and its path, so a caller that
    only wants to know which file was read stops here.
  - `config/parser.rs` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands it a string and never
    touches the filesystem.
    - the error type stays shared for now, since splitting it would change the messages
      `validate-config` prints and the acceptance check compares them
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field access moves behind the module
    boundary and the CLI no longer knows the file's shape.
```

The same cycle's ladder, `zTOC.md > ## Ladder`, made by the tool, linking across to the
subsections:

```
## Ladder

- 0 (done) [refactor: extract config loader opening](TODO.md#refactor-extract-config-loader-opening)
- 1 (current) [refactor: split loader from parser](TODO.md#refactor-split-loader-from-parser)
- [refactor: extract config loader closing](TODO.md#refactor-extract-config-loader-closing)
```

Its closing, `cycle --close --multi-step --trapezoid main`, makes the closing commit, every marker
`(done)` and the block moved whole to `## Closed`, its `#### Rungs` kept.

## A single-step cycle, closed

The `version flag` cycle, one commit made by `cycle --close --single-step`, as `TODO.md > ## Closed`
holds it:

```
## Closed

### feat: add a version flag

#### Problem

The binary has no way to say which version it is, so a bug report cannot name the build.

#### Solution

`-V` prints the name and the version-of-record, read at compile time.

#### Acceptance check

`<binary> -V` prints the version `Cargo.toml` holds.

#### Deliberation

_None._
```

There are no rung subsections: the scaffold wrote the bookends, and the closing dropped them, a
single-step cycle's one commit being neither. Its ladder is one unlinked rung with the bare title,
since a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's anchor:

```
## Ladder

- 0 (done) feat: add a version flag
```
